Chapter 14

← Chapter 13 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 15 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Musidora Tidings

Mr. Spitzer comes apart in this chapter, quietly and early. There are two Mr. Spitzers, then four brothers, then a "case of Spitzer versus Spitzer," and the shadowy doubles turn up in the playing cards whose suits become crosses and roses. This is the instability of male authority, and it is plural selfhood arriving in its central figure, a man who cannot be counted as one, litigating against himself across a deck of cards.

Catherine cannot say which of them is real and which imagined, and the not-knowing is the real and the dream as one country, the two versions equally present at her bedside.

Her fixation is the black coachman, who served the family in a role between the living and the dead and is now buried, and whom she insists on keeping present in full livery with his carriage and horses. This is the invisible labor of the servant and the erased figure of the minority, and it is the book's practice with the erased: it keeps them at the threshold, present and unaccounted for, the coachman held at the seam between life and death exactly as Musidora was and as Martha will be.

Spitzer names himself a "lost soul" in a woman's world, and the phrase is not only his defeat. It is a man reaching the same dissolving bottom the women reach, which is why he belongs at the center and not at the margin. His talk of law as the "practice of liars," of a cosmic harmony beyond human law, is the book setting aside the whole apparatus of sorting, the counting and owning and judging, for a world where the categories no longer hold.
woman-why-a-second-edition:
Why a second edition

Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · The Route Down →

The first edition of this book did a straightforward thing. It took Miss MacIntosh, My Darling seriously as a novel about women, placed it among the women experimentalists whose work had been pushed off the record, and traced the ways the book refuses to hold its shapes still. That work was right, and this edition keeps it. A reader who owns the first edition has lost nothing.

What sent me back to the book was a suspicion that the first reading had stopped too soon. It saw that the novel dissolves things. It named some of what dissolves: character running into character, scene into scene, the living into the dead. But it treated that dissolving as one feature among many, a matter of style and form, something the prose does on its way to its real subject. The longer I stayed with the novel, the more that got the order backward. The dissolution is not a feature of the book. It is the book. Everything else, the women, the reproductive range, the suffrage captain, the opium dreams, is the route Young takes to reach it.

The thing she reaches is a depth of consciousness that most fiction does not go near. She goes down into a mind and keeps going, past the point where the ordinary supports hold, until the categories a reader carries into the book stop working. Living and dead, waking and dreaming, man and woman, one self and the many selves inside it: each of these comes apart under the pressure of how far she is willing to go. This is not something the novel argues. It is something it does, sentence by sentence, across the eighteen years of its writing.

Once that is taken seriously, it cannot be added to the first edition as one more chapter. It changes what the other chapters are about. The book had been sorted into themes, women's bodies, marriage, grief, madness, and each theme had been read as a social condition the novel documents. All of that is still here, and all of it is still true. But under each theme is the same floor, and the floor is the same in every case: a self that will not stay single, in a world that will not stay sorted. The themes are the doors. The dissolution is the room they all open onto. To read the book that way is to read it again from the beginning, which is what a second edition is for.

This is why the novel's own line has moved to the center of this edition. "Every heart is the other heart. Every soul is the other soul. The individual is the one illusion." In the first edition that line could sit among the others, one striking sentence in a book full of them. Here it is the thesis, stated by the book about itself. The individual, the bounded single self that can be counted and sorted and owned, is the one thing the novel does not believe in, and everything it does to its women, and later to its men, is in the service of showing that the individual was never there to begin with.

The vocabulary this edition brings for that floor is new, and I want to be clear about its status before the chapters begin.
woman-chapter-45:
Chapter 45

← Chapter 44 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 46 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Joachim Spitzer

The woman the record cannot hold returns, and her unreachability is the pillar. The suffragette is a "great wanderer" who never answered his knocks or letters, her "empty house" the barren landscape of a life that would not be pinned to marriage or memory, and Mr. Spitzer's craving for certainty meets only her ambiguity. "Love's image was that which was never reached by love" turns the unattainable into the chapter's law, and her tears for a "clouded mirror," her refusal to reproduce herself, are a woman declining the reproductive destiny the world assigns her.

Her secret dual and triple life is the plural, contested selfhood the novel prizes, and Mr. Spitzer's disbelief that she was "no one in whom one should place his already shattered faith" is patriarchy's failure to hold a woman who lives past its categories. The volumes of lovelorn letters she never answered make her a repository of human longing she cannot or will not satisfy, "brides even when there were no loves," and the image names the illusions of marriage and the solitude of the woman who refuses them.

Beneath the deathbed visions runs the fracture of female solidarity. Her broken "eternal troth," the abandoned "girl's hand," and her contradictory claim to have both let go and been abandoned, are the personal costs of a life given to a public cause, loyalty strained by commitment. Her wandering through deserts and mountains, her message that "he who loves shall lose himself in love as in death," carries feminism's internationalism and its knowledge that love and loss are one motion. The chapter closes on mountains, snow, and the "roaring sea shell," the harsh and mysterious terrain of a woman's life, with Mr. Spitzer the silent mourner who could not reach her while she lived, and the record still open where she should have been kept.
woman-chapter-68:
Chapter 68

← Chapter 67 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 69 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Miss MacIntosh · Mr. Weed · Vera Cartwheel

Vera reaches the village at night, and real and dream as one country and the dissolving boundary between life and death organize what she finds. A place known only by daylight, the text says, is never known as it is, and this village of dilapidated buildings and "vacancy" and iridescent winter weeds is the ordinary town opening onto a dreamed one, the seam gone between the seen and the dreamed. The Tavern's "God's servants who were believers in the lamb," the sleeping man in a miner's hat "with no light in his bulb," the graveyard where the coal mines should be, hold the boundary open before anyone speaks, a village where the living and the dead keep the same address.

The Christian hangman, Mr. Weed, talks of tying knots that "none shall untie until Gabriel blows his horn," and the hangman's noose and the marital knots run together in his mouth so that marriage becomes a binding as final as an execution, the wedding and the funeral fused the way the book has fused them since Chapter 6. He calls death itself a "marriage ceremony" with life, and the metaphor carries marriage as social death and the boundary between living and dead giving way in a single figure, the rope and the ring the same knot.

His first wife, Marie, hanged herself while pregnant with a child she did not want, and his children "playing at hanging themselves" carry the cycle of female despair and reproductive dread down a generation, the interrupted and unwanted birth ending at the rope. His second wife wears the first wife's clothes, and the two women folded into one set of garments are the crossing and the doubling the book keeps performing, one woman worn over another, the dead wife present in the living one's dress, held at the threshold rather than let go.

The hangman's talk of "undiscovered crimes," of murderers who move like "sleep-walkers," of the "bedroom murders" that leave no clear author, is the diffusion of agency the book stated at the start, a death with no single hand behind it, the same logic that would not say who killed Miss MacIntosh. The woman who killed a man "for pleasure" and was spared the rope for her beauty, the man who murdered his wife over her cats and unraveled her identity by misspelling her letters, the black poker chip left at an unsolved killing, are the violence against women and the erasure of their voices the book keeps exposing, hidden in bedrooms and unaccounted for on the record. The hangman and the landlord climb the stairs, and Vera is left "rocking" below in a house with no clock to strike, suspended time closing the chapter on a woman waiting at the threshold while the men go up to their business.
woman-chapter-76:
Chapter 76

← Chapter 75 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 77 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Esther Longtree

Esther hides her "pupa, her Little Tom Thumb" in the mule's ear at the start of this chapter, wishing to disappear "under a small leaf," and the vulnerability she carries is the interrupted birth folded into a longing for erasure, a woman so exposed she would vanish under a flower. She names herself "widow often, an old maid always, a wife never," and the phrase is the social marginalization of a woman who fits none of the roles, and it is the plural, uncontainable self the book prefers, a person who is many things at once and cannot be filed as any single one.

Her stillborn children drift as "snowflakes drifting in eternity," "robes, bloodless," "hovering at the ivory gates between life and death," and the spectral infants are the interrupted birth turned into a haunting, the losses kept present at the threshold the book reserves for its dead. They intrude even on her intercourse, the "small brown hand moving over her, stealing her life," and the violation of past reproductive trauma into present sexuality is the book's boundary between life and death giving way inside the most intimate act.

The detective pursues her toward a trial for "mass infanticide," and Esther's realization that she "would strike at the living men" rather than the shadowy embryos turns the accusation back on the whole arrangement, a woman refusing to be the sole culprit of a violence men set in motion. Her memory that "her mother had killed her" carries the intergenerational transmission of guilt and harm, and the whole chapter is the diffusion of agency the book keeps insisting on, blame that will not settle on one hand because no loss here has a single author.

Esther calls herself the "best detective in the infinite," knitting a "black hood" for a child "white as melting snow," and the reclaiming of the investigator's role is a woman taking authorship of her own story back from the men who would file it. Her life is "monotonous" yet "beautiful and wild," and at the chapter's close she quits her job to "answer her own questions," a self-determination that refuses the surveillance and the trial alike, a woman who will hold her own inquiry rather than submit to the world's, and remain, pregnant always, the body the arrangement cannot close its case on.
woman-chapter-51:
Chapter 51

← Chapter 50 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 52 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Joachim Spitzer

The mute governs this chapter, and voicelessness is its pillar. A "mantle like the shell of mother-of-pearl" grows around consciousness, the nights unweave with no "loom" or "harp" to hold them, and the moon crosses as a "schooner" and a "lamp-lighter," and the historical silencing of women and the book's own erasure through severed sense arrive together, a self wrapped in a shell that cannot speak. Love here "was its own subject because it had no object," "dead love," "love which could not be born," running toward "doors leading nowhere" and a "darkened tower where no one lived," and the illusion of the individual, love with no separate object to fix on, is stated in the same breath as women's thwarted emotional lives.

Mr. Spitzer is "of neither world nor world," multiplying into doctor, lawyer, postman, lighthouse keeper, musician, "lawyer to starfish," "lawyer for a moon in the cloud," "old lamp-lighter," and the many roles are the fragmented, imposed self and the plural selfhood the book prefers to any single one. He signs wills, scatters "ink and sand," holds "power of attorney," acts "in another's place," and the acting-for-another is women's exclusion from legal personhood and it is the book's claim that no self is fully its own, each standing in for others. A "mouse" gnaws the documents and the musical manuscripts alike, the record and the song eroded together, invisibility working on both.

He is "woven from wrong chains," missing a "keyboard," missing a "string in the harp of God," burdened with "errors" and "sins" of spirit, and the fragmentation is the psychological cost of oppression and it is the body as the place the self comes apart, a person assembled wrong from the start. Illusion and mirage blur the real and the unreal, "blind Eros" loves past "the limitations of the individual," an umbrella of zodiac signs twirls time, and the woman's dismissed reality and the book's fused country of real and dream are one weather.

The chapter's sharpest figures are women crossing out of their assigned shapes. "Old women" believe themselves stags with antlers and fear the "man in a red coat," a reindeer-woman is found dead with a "golden arrow," an "old maid" cuckolds her husband, and the surveillance and violence women meet when they take non-normative forms and the crossing point, gender and species giving way, arrive as one dark comedy. "Obsessive loves" and "splittings" fuse identities in dream, living love and dead love and multiple selves running together, and Mr. Spitzer, evicted from the "citadel" where he hears "another heart above his heart," identifying with his dead twin, is the plural self at its most unhoused. The "careless dreamer" who is "the heart of God upon a world never created" closes the chapter on a feminine creative power still unrealized, a maker whose world was never let into being.
woman-chapter-15:
Chapter 15

← Chapter 14 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 16 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

On her fourteenth birthday Vera walks along the sea, and the sea is the chapter's whole argument. Its dissolving boundary between sky and water, its wreckage and lost statues, its upheaval, is the real and the dream as one country made elemental, the place where fixed things come apart. Vera embraces it. She wants the imperfection that leads to "higher perfection," she loses her fear of the "outer darkness," and she gives in to the pull of the water.

Miss MacIntosh cannot follow her there. She cannot swim, she bundles against the cold, she keeps clear of the "greatest waves," and the narrator reads in her a "coldness of heart," a "deadness." She is the pole that resists dissolution, and her refusal of the sea is the setup for the day she will walk straight into it. Her austere room holds the tell: an abandoned dressing table, a woman who will not look in her mirror, "shades of death" already on her. The refusal to meet her own image is the body and the self coming apart held just out of sight, the face she will not look at the same one whose wig and baldness the book is preparing to reveal.

Miss MacIntosh’s counsel is bleak and against the sorting. Death is a "bridegroom," marriage a "padlock," men "poor, forked animals," and "no man should marry woman." Vera answers it with a "secret dream of the false wedding" to Mr. Spitzer, a surreal ceremony attended by natural and supernatural forces, the crossing point returning as a dream, the wedding to a dissolving man staged again in the mind that most wants the fixed to give way. The old blind sheep dog barks at the waves at the chapter's edge, a severed sense set against the dissolving sea, and the two together are the book in miniature.
woman-chapter-54:
Chapter 54

← Chapter 53 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 55 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer

The underwater dream opens this chapter, and the dissolving of every boundary is its pillar. The opium lady's dreams open a "vast subterranean unconscious," a sea of "fertility and transformation," and Mr. Spitzer moves through it as the passive interpreter of a world a woman has dreamed into being, real and dream as one country with a woman at its source. His brother's death and the "alien acquaintances" rattling his conscience, Peron's "chaotic sound and disorder" against Joachim's "silence and order," set the two brothers going again, and the sound effects man who makes "chaos through vocal cords" is the disruptive liminal figure the book keeps placing at the margins, a self performing its own noise.

Insomnia fills the chapter with phantom sounds, bees and birds and natural music, feminine-coded and cyclical, and Mr. Spitzer is "deaf" or "dead" to them, the severed sense that the book uses for erasure turned inward on the man estranged from the living world. He mistakes himself for his dead brother, the reality and the illusion blurring, and the confusion is plural selfhood at its most literal, a self that cannot tell itself from its double. Streets shift and landscapes alter, time and identity go fluid, and all the fixed categories the book keeps refusing, a city that will not hold its shape.

Marginalized figures crowd the chapter, old women and "ragged tramps," and Mr. Spitzer as "finder of lost heirs" and helper of the abandoned carries the book's care for the erased, the relational ethic it keeps setting against the ledger. Women disguised as men, "Indian maidens," a woman "dressing as a man to survive," bring the crossing point and gender as performance into the crowd, surviving wearing the other sex the way the suffragette did. His refusal "to own real jewels," his suspicion as a jewel thief, his self-imposed exile under accusation, are the scapegoating and social ostracism the book knows women and the marginalized by, and the network of "sightings and rumors" is the surveillance that pins a body it cannot recognize.

Death and legacy close it. Mr. Spitzer's admiration for Peron against his own isolation, his search for self and brother, his ambivalence about "love, identity, eternity," are the fragile masculine self the book keeps unmaking, and the "two wrist watches," one for the living and one for the dead, hold the coexistence of multiple selves and times in a single object. Peron's song and Spitzer's fear at hearing it set self against other, life against death, order against chaos, homecoming against loss, and the chapter ends with Mr. Spitzer as the composer of his life's music, "fragmentary and unfinished," the interrupted work the book gives its people in place of any whole.
woman-chapter-35:
Chapter 35

← Chapter 34 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 36 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer

Cousin Hannah out-plays Mr. Spitzer at cards, and that small mastery opens the chapter's pillar: female authority inverting male power, the woman commanding a domain the man cannot read. His suspicion that she cheats because he cannot follow the game, his cynicism that "death would not improve her honesty," is the distrust that meets women who excel, and Catherine's admiration of Hannah's honor answers it. Against his bitterness and jealousy, his passivity, Hannah is active, audacious, unyielding, the "corporeal" obstacle of Mr. Spitzer set against a woman who commanded respect even from historical male authorities.

The chapter imagines her sovereign, a house of "vacant rooms" and "gilded footmen" ready to serve her, a reversal that puts a woman in power with men attending, and it frames suffrage as her one consuming love. She is the "true love" of the cause, wanting no romance or domesticity, and her all-consuming activism, her travels and confrontations, her riding "through deserts and cold lands" against "despotic, one-eyed ogres," makes feminism a transnational siege. She rejects the "old maid" stereotype not by marrying but by refusing the frame entirely, and her knowledge of "why explorers and husbands leave home" exposes the coldness inside domestic life, the unawakened woman whose heart has never been reached.

What sets her apart from Catherine is unity: Hannah has "no internal conflicts that divided her," her enemy is "physical rather than psychological," while Catherine's self is fragmented into dream and rivalry. The chapter credits Hannah's focused resistance without pretending it costs nothing; her fear that "yielding once would mean permanent defeat" names the stakes and the strain together. Catherine's tentative wish to understand the suffrage message "now, after years of resistance," registers feminist consciousness slowly permeating even the dreamer, so that the separation between the two women begins, barely, to close. The chapter ends on Hannah's "hardy temper" and "contempt for physical hazard," a woman whose courage the novel names outright, and whose singular purpose stands as its own answer to a world that divides women against themselves.
woman-decolonization-in-miss-macintosh-m:
Decolonization in Miss MacIntosh, My Darling

← Young's contribution to feminist thought · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · A closing word →

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Esther Longtree · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh

Decolonization in literature is the work of dismantling the Eurocentric and imperial assumptions built into the canon, reclaiming the voices and narratives that colonial storytelling erased or subordinated. Young was not writing a decolonial program, and the book is not organized around one. Yet the pushback is real and it runs through the novel, sometimes as a pointed line against the Empire and its histories, and at its deepest as the same refusal that drives everything else in the book, the refusal to let any single account, imperial or historical or individual, stand as the whole.

The direct critique is plain enough. Miss MacIntosh condemns the "British Empire" and sets herself against "the exploitations of the natives and of the workers in the dark Satanic mills," and Mr. Spitzer's grief reaches "what America had done to passenger pigeons" and "to Indians in their lonely tepees." The passenger pigeon is not a decoration here. Martha, the last of her kind, mourned in the novel only by an old black porter, is the book's emblem of the erased, and setting the slaughtered pigeons beside the dispossessed of the tepees names colonial destruction and species extinction with one grief, the vanished kept at the threshold where the book keeps all its dead.

The novel also strips the authority from the West's founding stories. Columbus is dismissed as a "mere pretender," since "many an old sailor had already been washed up here and did not live to talk about it," and Cook and Peary would have done "better as fiction writers." This is the failure of the record turned on the record's proudest pages, the discoverer revealed as a latecomer to a place that was never lost, the explorer's claim exposed as a story told well enough to be believed. Young's suspicion of any account that presents itself as the whole truth, which runs through Catherine's dream and Spitzer's watches and the book's whole blurring of what is real, lands here on imperial history and dissolves its confidence.

Esther Longtree's story carries the racial injustice most directly. Her lover is a "Negro" who fled the South and its "white people," and the "white detective" who haunts her, "hating all things black," ignores the murders of "little black children" because he deems them "unimportant." The line the detective draws through justice, investigating the white child and abandoning the black one, is the intersecting erasure the book performs elsewhere with Martha and the mute and the coachman, the marginal life kept present precisely because the official world will not account for it.

Cousin Hannah folds the colonial reversal and the patriarchal one into a single figure. She rides "disguised as an Arab king," driving "the courtly Spanish cavalcades... before her like chickens," a reversal of the conquest narrative in which the European column is routed by a woman in the dress of the colonized, and her lifelong war for the "overthrow of man" and "paternal domination" is the crossing point meeting the anti-colonial inversion, gender and empire overturned in the same ride. Mr. Spitzer's conviction that the world "was woman's world from the beginning" sits beside her as the quiet form of the same claim, and Hannah's scorn for explorers who name their discoveries after their wives catches the patriarchal habit folded inside the colonial one.

The book's aversion to Western progress runs alongside. Miss MacIntosh's hatred of "electric lights" and modern convenience, and her disdain for the "civilized corruption" that overtakes the head-hunter once he is exposed to Western refinement, invert the civilizing mission outright, the refinement figured as the corruption and the so-called savage as the one it spoils. The reach is worth naming as a reach: this is the book's broad suspicion of a certain idea of progress as much as a developed postcolonial argument, and it works by feel and reversal rather than by program. It is real, and it is a temperament more than a thesis.

The deepest decolonizing move is none of these lines. It is the novel's refusal of the individual. "Every heart is the other heart. Every soul is the other soul," the book insists, and "the individual is the one illusion," and this is the illusion of the individual, the central pillar of the whole reading, stated in a form that happens also to be anti-colonial to its root. The sovereign, bounded, self-owning individual is the unit colonial order runs on, the figure who discovers and claims and names and owns, and when Young dissolves that individual she pulls the ground out from under the arrangement more completely than any single line against the Empire could. Her interconnectedness, the communal and holistic understanding of existence the book keeps returning to, is where her consciousness work and her decolonizing work turn out to be one work. She goes deep enough into the self that the self dissolves, and the self that dissolves is the one colonialism required.
woman-chapter-79:
Chapter 79

← Chapter 78 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 80 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Esther Longtree

A silver spoon made Esther in this chapter, and the crossing point runs through the story of her conception. Her mother and father never consummated their marriage, a "blushing bride" who never matured and an immense passive man, and a third person carried the seed between them with the spoon, so that Esther's origin is a thought "rather than a fact," the interrupted birth run backward into the very act of conceiving her. The mother's fragility against the father's bulk, the union that was never a union, is the loveless marriage the book keeps exposing, a honeymoon with no consummation stretched across a life.

The go-between is an "old concubine" who carries the spoon, monstrous and powerful, dressed in masculine attire and foreign, and her ambiguous gender is the crossing point set at the source of Esther's life, the seam the book writes from present at the moment of her making. When the revelation comes that this "other woman" was in fact a man who "deflowered" the mother in disguise, the crossing point turns to violation and deception at once, gender used as a mask over an assault, the man wearing the woman to reach a woman.

The conception takes seven years of pain and dread while the father sits "reading baseball scores," and the gap between his obliviousness and her mother's torment is the uneven burden of reproduction the book keeps weighing, the man untouched while the woman is worked on. The mother's conflicted feelings, her attempts to abort, the violent birth in which Esther is "born kicking," are the interrupted birth turned nearly to its opposite, a delivery resisted from both sides, and the mother's scorn afterward and Esther's guilt for "killing the shadow" carry the fracture forward into the daughter.

Esther's identity stays split between herself and the "shadow," the stillborn potential the book keeps doubling her with, plural selfhood carried from the womb, and the multiplicity of "fathers," the "puny salesmen," scatters her paternity the way her selfhood is scattered. When she confronts the dying go-between who is "the father," the illusions of family and love and origin die with the figure, and Esther's own "gradual death," her talking "of dead grasshoppers," close the chapter on a woman connected to the dying natural world, coming apart slowly and speaking to the dead, at home in the country where real and dream are one.
woman-chapter-16:
Chapter 16

← Chapter 15 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 17 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Falada · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Vera rides Falada, her old black pony, through the ruined garden on her birthday, and the ride locates her mind outside her body. Falada carries the name of the speaking horse's head from the fairy tale, and Vera says the horse "seemed to be my head, my intelligence," which makes her "the headless rider." This is a girl's exhilaration and freedom, and it is the detachable self, the intelligence set loose from the body and carried by an animal, the head motif the book has run since the head-hunter wanted Miss MacIntosh's and the villagers grew heads beneath their shoulders. The self here is distributed between rider and horse, plural before Vera has even dismounted.

She dreams herself into other bodies as she rides, a comedian with a mustache, a bareback rider in pink tights, and the mustache is the crossing point tucked into a daydream, gender tried on and set down. Falada goes "winged" over church steeples, the ordinary pony transcending the solid world, real and dream as one country.

The ride ends at the tomb-like house, its marble courts, its "garden of the blind," its silence over still water, a place where erasure and the dead are the weather. Vera passes Catherine asleep among sea shells and "little fish sleepers" and goes instead to Miss MacIntosh's door. The web on the doorknob, the creak, the moonbeams, and then recognition with an "older shock" underneath it: the changed woman is already waiting, and the chapter ends a breath before the book shows what the change is.
woman-chapter-56:
Chapter 56

← Chapter 55 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 57 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer

Clothing is the chapter's whole preoccupation, and the mask made of cloth is its pillar. Mr. Spitzer dresses his dead brother for the funeral, choosing the formal swallow-tail over the loud checkered suits Peron wore alive, dressing the corpse "like himself" and not like the man it was, and the performance is masculinity constructed from the outside, the self as mask, gender kept up by what a body is wrapped in even after the body has stopped. The poker chips and dice and racing forms laid in as "coins" to pay the ferry boatman tie manhood to gambling and risk and sport, and death made "a formal occasion" requiring proper dress is the performative self carried across the boundary between life and death, the mask worn to the far shore.

The funeral crowds with male ritual, musicians and a bugler, the "official track bugler" whose prestigious career marks the patriarchal institutional power that presides over mourning, and against it Mr. Spitzer imagines his own funeral of "lyres and harps" made of flowers, delicate and feminine-coded, the crossing point tucked into a daydream of how he would rather be buried. Peron himself is a "squid changing colors and evading capture," a self that will not be pinned to one shape, and the shape-shifting is the plural selfhood the book carries in the brothers, gender and identity both refusing to hold still.

Mr. Spitzer gives Peron's clothing away, the hunting jackets and jockey suits, the hats and scarves, the "ass's head" hat and Balaklava helmets, the jewel-colored jockey suits and medieval clown costumes distributed to homeless men, and the dispersal of a wardrobe is the dispersal of a self and a legacy, clothing as the layers of a gender that comes apart when its wearer does. The tiny "dwarf's suit" among them, and Spitzer's question of who mourns the small and fragile, is the book's care for the marginalized and the non-normative, and his grief that "mourned for everything," breaking the lines between subject and object, life and death, self and other, is the illusion of the individual dissolving in a widower's blurred sight.

Reality itself goes "unreal" for him here, a "dead man walking," Spitzer and Peron interchangeable, appearances all clouds and shadows and changing colors, and the absence of any true "being" underneath is the constructed, mutable self the book prefers to any essence. Barnacles and seaweed cling to him, "all things, being none," and he asks the tailor who clothed him whether he is a "poor puppet" or a "tailor's dummy," a self with no author, holding a "golden key" to a door that is "no more." The chapter ends on the dead musician who keeps singing, the "demented sea shells," the "silken skies torn in two," the music that goes unheard sounding past the death of the one who made it, and no architect anywhere to have made either the man or the world he mourns in.
woman-chapter-77:
Chapter 77

← Chapter 76 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 78 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Esther Longtree

The chapter opens on a cosmic scale of blame, "who killed the heavens," the "green earth," "love," and the diffusion of agency the book keeps stating is raised here to the size of the sky. Esther's private tragedy, the deaths of her children and her unheard cries, is written across the whole of creation, and "everybody else" who "had done wrong" bringing unwanted children into the world is set against her, who "had done no wrong" because she "wanted children," the interrupted birth reframed as the one honest desire in a world of forced and resented ones. The "great, overhanging veil" the doctor names is the social and existential weight pressing on a woman's reproductive life, and Esther's spine "curved by the weight of memory" carries it in her body.

The flour miller's story of the "thumb print" that cannot be inherited on the flour is the failure of the record to hold a life, an identity that leaves no lasting mark, and the "little book" Esther finds rain-stained and buried is the lost knowledge and silenced testimony the book keeps unearthing, a message from the dead or the unborn. Its alphabet becomes "exhibits" that accuse her, "Mother, why did you kill me?", the letters A through U arraigning her, and the reduction of a woman's reproductive losses to evidence in a trial is the legal machinery the book keeps exposing, motherhood surveilled and prosecuted rather than witnessed.

The detective investigates only "little white children" and ignores the deaths of "little black children" because he "hated the black," and the racial line drawn through justice is the intersecting erasure the book has carried since Martha the passenger pigeon, whose loss the old black porter alone mourned. That the detective finds both a white and a black child and retreats is society's selective empathy made stark, the black child's death unrecorded and unavenged, and Esther's own child by a black father places her inside that erasure, a woman whose motherhood crosses the line the law refuses to cross.

The story of the "mass murderess" abortionist who killed poor unmarried mothers and their babies, who murdered even a woman "pregnant in her dreams," is the danger women face in a world that condemns and criminalizes their reproductive lives, the interrupted birth turned to slaughter. Esther's reflection that "parts of us must die even as we are conceived" folds the boundary between life and death into the very act of creation, and her question "Should a woman ever answer a man's questions?" closes the chapter on a refusal of the whole interrogation, a woman keeping her mystery against a surveillance that has no page for her and no justice for the children it decides do not count.
woman-chapter-61:
Chapter 61

← Chapter 60 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 62 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer · Musidora Tidings

A frog does the mute's talking in this chapter, and voicelessness is the pillar it carries. The mute cannot speak and keeps a frog trained to croak words in his place, everyday cautions like "Watch out for the pickpockets," and the rented croak is the historical silencing of women and the book's erasure through a severed sense arriving as one thing, a man with no voice of his own who must borrow one from an animal. When the frog dies the silence closes over him by exactly the sound it loses, and the book keeps him at the threshold the way it keeps all its erased, present and unaccounted for, the almost-seen and almost-heard figure who runs from Musidora through the black coachman and Martha into a body that cannot speak at all.

The frog's death and its long burial give the chapter its grief, and the grief is carried in gesture because it cannot be carried in words. The mute's hands, "white as lilies," sign division and prayer and meeting and parting and flight, a whole language "like fish fins waving through water," and the sign language is the alternative expression the book keeps crediting to the silenced, plural selfhood spoken with the body when the throat is shut. The wild flora around the grave, its fertility and its natural cycles, set life against the mute's stopped voice, and Mr. Spitzer mourning beside him without fully understanding him is the male witness half-comprehending a grief he did not make, the same half-understanding he brought to Cousin Hannah's deathbed.

Mr. Spitzer envies the mute his silence, "free from the discords, alarms, irritating buzzings" of sound, and the envy is the book naming silence as a refuge and not only a wound. Yet he grieves that the mute has "missed music and law and conceptions of justice," and the two feelings together are the double bind the book keeps finding, the silenced person spared the noise of the world and shut out of its institutions in the same stroke, refuge and exclusion arriving as one condition.

The mute walks "like a traveller in a foreign country," present in a hearing world and cut off from it, invisibility and erasure worked into a man who cannot be reached by the sound around him. And Mr. Spitzer, the "mournful musician" whose compositions no one hears, finds in the mute his "ideal audience," the listener who cannot listen, so that the music that goes unheard meets the ear that cannot hear it and the book's two great absences fold into one scene. The chapter ends on silence as "greater than sound," the unspoken carrying more than the spoken, and it leaves the mute among the many in an eternal silence that is loss and peace at once, refusing to make the reader choose between them.
woman-chapter-57:
Chapter 57

← Chapter 56 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 58 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Peron Spitzer

A tailor's bill drives this chapter, and the debt that will not close is its pillar. Mr. Spitzer owes for the black funeral suit, and the accounting of funeral expenses, the honor and debt and legacy, is the masculine order of ledgers, and the tailor who made the suit, a male "figure of creation and transformation," stands for patriarchy's power to cut and shape a self from the outside. That the tailor may never have existed, or is dead, is the collapse of the very certainty the ledger depended on, the real and the dream running together so that the man who owes cannot find the man he owes.

The letters Mr. Spitzer opens carry the chapter's women. "Old Floradora girls" with "matted horse-hair wigs" and "eyeballs distended with bella donna" are the marginalized femininity of performance and aging and decay, entertainers whose value faded when their youth did, and the horse-hair wigs are the self as mask again, the detachable covering the book keeps returning to since Miss MacIntosh's own. Spitzer, "enclosed in a sea shell" while Peron went free, is male confinement inside societal expectation, and his "burning point" against the tailor's insult to his integrity is the social reputation and masculine pride the book keeps naming so it can watch them dissolve.

The search for the tailor takes him through a shifting dreamlike city of "contradictory signs and illusions," and the navigation of masks and false facades is real and dream as one country, a man looking for a stable identity and a fixed street and finding neither. He cannot retrace his steps, cannot map his own history, and seeing his reflection "like the pigeon's watery murmur" is the fragile, unstable self-recognition the book gives everyone who looks for a single self and finds a rippling one. The city directories and maps that hold no tailor and no street are the record failing to keep a life, women's absence from the archive and the book's larger erasure the same failure, and the thought of hiring an "Indian guide" pulls colonial and racial dispossession into the same lost ground.

Obituary and society news set men's public achievements beside women's social appearances, and the "famous beauty" who abandoned society and is presumed dead is the boundary between life and death held open on a woman reported gone because she stopped being seen. The old librarian, comically inept with a string of spectacles "one for every kind of distance" and always the wrong pair, is a female authority made outdated and ineffective, and the library's Bedlam, the people talking to themselves, the "living and dead men debating the soul's existence," is the fractured modern world with its patriarchal order coming undone. The Confederate veteran insisting on a bullet from Appomattox that could not be there is historical myth-making the book meets with a "sympathetic nod as if a high wind were blowing," and the chapter closes on clouds as moths shifting into skulls and birds and roses, a rose named for Spitzer "proud that he was faithful," red and white grafted on one bush, transformation and multiplicity flowering where the fixed self was supposed to stand.
woman-chapter-30:
Chapter 30

← Chapter 29 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 31 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Eustace

Eustace opens the chapter as pure fluidity, invisible and shapeshifting, "mocking bird, old man, old woman, military figures," and this refusal of fixed form is the pillar Young then hands to Cousin Hannah. Catherine's private communication with a presence no one else can see is the isolation of a woman whose nonconforming vision goes unwitnessed, and her wish for card partners like Cousin Hannah, who can be "two partners at once," turns that isolation toward multiplicity as power rather than deficit.

Cousin Hannah enters as the transgressive figure the whole novel has been circling. She refuses the Spitzer brothers and forecasts their ruin; she carries a worldly knowledge of "politics, assassinations, and royal intrigues" the domestic sphere was built to keep from women; she will not settle, will not take long visits or telephone calls, and treats mobility itself as a claim against confinement. Her feats cross every boundary Eustace's shapeshifting anticipated: archer, dueler, marksman, mountain climber, jockey, disguised "as an Arab king," riding "against the courtly Spanish cavalcades, driving them before her like chickens." The shedding of "a skirt," mourned and redeemed, is the shedding of an imposed femininity, and her impatience and decisiveness, her power to cut "great cables of iron" and "silken threads," are the traits patriarchy codes masculine reclaimed for a woman who will not be governed.

This is radical female agency and it is the novel's insistence that "the individual is the one illusion," the two meeting in a single figure. Hannah moves through disguise and self-multiplication the way the book moves through overlapping identities; Catherine calls her an "emancipated extension" of herself, so that the two women are one refusal wearing two bodies. Her survival past hired assassins, her strategic navigation of "one-eyed ogres greater than death," her dedication to "the overthrow of the dream and of the dreamer," set active resistance against Catherine's opium escape without letting either cancel the other. The chapter closes on the image of sailing "two ships" at once, one for the living and one for the dead, the dual reality every woman navigates, and it treats that doubleness as command rather than division.
woman-chapter-62:
Chapter 62

← Chapter 61 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 63 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Joachim Spitzer

Mr. Spitzer writes his own will in this chapter, and the music that goes unheard is what he wills away. The dream opens it, rivers of fire and ice, old seals in "diamond necklaces with diamond crosses," seagulls turning into musicians with human faces, and the transforming dreamworld is real and dream as one country, the sea a place where instruments and animals and people trade shapes. Then the will: he leaves his compositions "to the musical world and even to indifferent ears and even to deaf ears," and the bequest to the deaf is the music that goes unheard handed forward on purpose, a legacy addressed to the very absence that will not receive it.

A pack rat steals and exchanges the objects and the manuscripts, and the theft is the book's erasure working on the record itself, women's unacknowledged and appropriated labor carried by a small thief in the walls. The music cannot be realized, thwarted by "atmospheric and environmental factors," and its titles name what will never sound, a "Pavanne for the Dead Polar Bear and the Entombed Butterfly," the unplayed piece mourning a loss it cannot perform. Its "music of the dead," its inscrutable codes and "counter-worlds," are the non-dominant expression the book keeps crediting, the composition that exists "apart from transitory sound" and defies the categories that would let it be heard.

The chapter's players are all broken in the same way, undone by the very art that defines them. The old horn-blower keeps playing though tuberculosis is killing him, devotion destroying the devotee; the clarinetist takes his own life over the fear of being "out of tune," the impossibility of a perfect self-presentation turned fatal; the old violinist dances and plays with no instrument at all, the music existing only where no one but Mr. Spitzer can find it. The second violinist is the sharpest of them, a man who "never touched the strings," who deceived the audience for years and was dismissed for a single false note, and his invisibility and precariousness are the book's erasure in a concert seat, the player present and unaccounted for until one error erases him entirely.

Mr. Spitzer identifies with "the sad dead millions," a single man carrying many voices, and the identification is the illusion of the individual stated over a will, the self that is not one distributing itself across everyone it mourns. The chapter closes on music as silence, on the beauty of what goes unplayed and unheard, and it leaves the whole apparatus of performance and audience set aside for a sound that needs no ear, the unheard song the book keeps composing for its erased, willed forward here to a world it trusts will never hear it and left, all the same, as the only legacy worth leaving.
woman-chapter-43:
Chapter 43

← Chapter 42 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 44 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Joachim Spitzer

A man arrives at understanding too late, and that lateness is the pillar. Mr. Spitzer carries the dying suffragette through a storm he cannot help her against, "voicing the music of the dead," and his confusion about whom he mourns, whether he is alive or dead, is the difficulty of witnessing and preserving a feminist life from outside it. His abstention from voting, his line that "the dead cast no vote," folds women's disenfranchisement into the scene, and his understanding that "always came too late" is the culture's chronic lateness to the women who fought for it.

The suffragette's delirium holds the fracture of a feminist self. Her "returning loves," the desires she had "subdued" and "denied," surface at the end and name the tension between private longing and public duty that a life of struggle demands, and her cry "Who am I? Am I myself or another heart?" is the plural, interconnected selfhood the novel keeps opening, identity dissolving under the weight of the cause and the world's expectations. Her weeping at a snowflake, her fear of the "unknown, untried, unknowable," expose the vulnerability beneath the warrior, and the narrator's sense that "few could endure the absolute truth" while "most must be self-deceived" measures the loneliness of seeing clearly in a society that will not.

The chapter reaches across history and race for its scope. Her fragmented invocations of ancient cities and armies place feminism in a long human continuum, and her cries for "Black Moor" and "golden archer" widen it past gender into racial and cultural intersection. Death here is ending and transformation at once, the "lid" she cannot tell is "lowering or raising," the boundary held open. The chapter closes on Mr. Spitzer piecing broken mosaics he grasps only after the fact, and on a feminist life that stays a journey through storm and contradiction, with no clean resolution and a persistent reaching toward meaning.
woman-chapter-26:
Chapter 26

← Chapter 25 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 27 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer

The chapter runs on the machinery of law, and law is the pillar: the instrument by which a woman's property, her illness, and her existence pass into the keeping of men. Mr. Spitzer administers "the dead" and "hidden pasts," and the estates he settles are full of people "who were rich and imagined they were poor, those who were poor and imagined they were rich," a confusion of status that falls hardest on women, whose class is never their own but arrives through a man. The women who write "many wills to baffle even the most conscientious attorney" are practicing the only authorship the system leaves them, scrambling the record so that no clean line of inheritance can be drawn through their hands. This is women's dispossession under inheritance law and it is the failure of the record itself to hold a woman's life, the two being the same failure.

Against that failure Young sets the Boston lady who believes she is Cleopatra reborn and leaves everything to her Siamese cats. She reclaims a female power the histories have maligned and she routes her legacy outside the male line entirely, to creatures with "nine lives" who own her house after her death. Legacy passes without lineage: the cats persist where daughters and heirs do not, and female continuity survives in a form the law was not built to recognize. Mr. Spitzer, "never amused by life," cannot follow her into that magic; his rational, conservative custody stands for everything that measures and forecloses, and her feline immortality escapes his ledgers.

Catherine is the case that gathers all of this. She is "already dead" in the eyes of the men who manage her, kept and controlled through debts and sedatives while her brother's rivalry and neglect compound her suffering. Mr. Spitzer's loyalty to her, unreturned, and his "ideal and incorruptible marriage" that "never could have been" in the flesh, name marriage and law together as institutions that promise women shelter and deliver confinement. His nightwatch over the "lower world" of thieves and "street women," the passage one must cross to reach "the upper world," admits the whole marginalized economy of women the respectable order refuses to see. The chapter closes on that admission and does not soften it: to reach any legitimate world one goes through the streets where women are least protected and most surveilled, and the law that files the wills has no page for them.
woman-chapter-40:
Chapter 40

← Chapter 39 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 41 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah

Voice is the pillar, and Young gives it to Cousin Hannah as a spirit who speaks languages "no living person had ever spoken." Armored, with a "Gothic cathedral voice" and a "husky baritone," fluent in dead and mystical tongues, she is the reclamation of silenced knowledge and the "proud suffragette" whose speech itself shakes cloud ceilings and cracks mirrors, so that a woman's voice becomes a force that unsettles the built world. Catherine's wonder at why Hannah should speak at all registers how thoroughly women have been silenced, and how radical the plain fact of her voice is.

Non-linear time is the pillar's second face. Hannah's fury at archaeologists and "believers in linear time," the sense that "all of space could be wound, unwound like a bolt of silk," refuses the straight patriarchal chronology, and Catherine's fluency in languages she never studied is the innate, intuitive knowledge a male education system withheld from women. The disruption of natural order, echo before song and death before life, is the deconstruction of the sequences that hold women in place, and the mingling of living and dead is women's particular relation to memory and loss.

Hannah learns by observing rather than by instruction, greeting strangers as relatives, keeping "silent conversations" with figures like Daniel Boone and an opossum "feigning death," and her adventures may be spiritual and mental as much as physical, the inner life patriarchal history overlooks. Catherine's mind, an "iridescent jumble" of unthought thoughts and unlived dreams, and her uncertain physical presence, whether she has walked out into the clouds, are the fluid, uncontainable feminine selfhood the chapter refuses to pin down. It ends on water flowing over "mooned sand" and the figurehead who knows more than the captain, a woman seen as ornament possessing the deeper knowledge, and the voice that was never supposed to be heard still speaking.
woman-chapter-53:
Chapter 53

← Chapter 52 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 54 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer

Two brothers hold this chapter, and their doubling is the pillar. Mr. Spitzer's identity fragments against Peron's, his delicate sensitivity set against the roles a man is handed, composer and gambler and mourner, and the fragmentation is the fragile masculine self and the plural selfhood the book carries in its central man. He is alienated, the boundaries between life and death and self and other gone blurry, missed connections and passing trains marking the openings a fixed self keeps missing, and Peron's "brilliant," many-colored life against Joachim's "colorless" one is the difference between two ways of being handed to men, neither of them whole.

The mourning cloak and the black keyboard set the chapter's key. Mr. Spitzer wants "equilibrium between opposing forces," life and death, acceptance and rejection, and the wish for balance is the book's refusal to let the binaries stand, the seam it writes from named in a man's grief. He wanders the city among "twin rooms and double arrangements," "twins" and "mirrors" everywhere, and the doubling is plural selfhood and the mirror in which a self is made against its opposite. His knowledge of gambling and sports and fighting fills male-dominated arenas with cards and dice and blows, and the absence of women from them marks the gendered division the book keeps noting, even as the fighters "broken by life" and the men who become "widows" of themselves undo the toughness those arenas were built to prove.

The chameleon and the "many-colored cloth" carry the crossing point. Identity here is performance, masks and disguises and assumed selves, and the political figure who was biologically female and lived as a man, who died and was buried in social ambiguity, is the crossing point at its most consequential, the policing of gender boundaries and the erasure of the gender-nonconforming staged in a single life. Men become "widows" of themselves, fighters become "madames" or "babysitters," and the porous line between masculinity and femininity runs through the whole chapter.

The arbitrariness of knowledge closes it. Identities shift, music and chess moves stand in for the fixed self, the "black etude" and the "black keyboard" mark mourning and the possibility of new composition beyond the old forms, and the fluidity is the book's rejection of the single, essential self. Peron's chameleon adaptability against Spitzer's "black velvet melancholy" leaves two brothers who are two faces of one unwillingness to be counted as one, and the chapter ends inside their doubling, a man composing his life out of a brother he cannot tell himself apart from.
woman-chapter-32:
Chapter 32

← Chapter 31 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 33 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah

Two women stand for two ways of refusing, and their doubling is the pillar. Cousin Hannah brandishes "the strident clash of arms," fighting overwhelming battles for suffrage and emancipation, refusing to yield or to "simulate indifference as Catherine does"; Catherine keeps to her frail, dreamlike existence, her opium and her illusions. Militant action on one side and retreat into dream on the other are not opposites so much as two faces of a single unwillingness to accept the world as given, and Young holds both without ranking them into simple hero and failure.

Hannah is "the high-souled lover of woman," not a hater of men but a rescuer of women from subjugation, and her program to turn parasols and veils, the ornamental trappings of flirtation and fragility, into "weapons of offense or defense" is the reclaiming of female agency from decorative passivity. She is a "great courier of every storm," a global and historical force, and feminism in her is a worldwide siege, "storming castles" and corroding shores, persistent through repeated failure. The cost is named too: loneliness, the absence of romantic love, an "unsullied honor" preserved at the price of a solitary life. Feminist militancy exacts its price and the chapter does not hide it.

Catherine's surreal marriages, "sometimes to phantoms or natural elements," refuse conventional heterosexual roles from the other direction, elusiveness where Hannah offers confrontation. The chapter ends on the paradox of visibility and invisibility that dogs feminist struggle: Hannah dies "in bed and not upon the lonely battlefield," her public battles resolving into a private death, while Catherine longs to "die while travelling," to be transformed out of stasis. The two women's fates rhyme rather than contrast, and the doubling of action and dream, sacrifice and escape, is the chapter's finished figure for how women refuse a world that will not have them.
woman-chapter-34:
Chapter 34

← Chapter 33 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 35 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah

Catherine imagines herself married in black rather than white, and the inversion is the chapter's pillar: marriage as social death, the rite that should begin a life staged instead as its end. She cannot tell whether the ceremony is "a wedding, a funeral, or an auction," and the confusion is the whole feminist charge, marriage as a rite of passage that is also a passing away, the "death of a woman's soul" the great suffrage captain names. The prophetic St. Bernard delivering the Viaticum blurs the sacraments until the bride's forward motion into marriage and her motion toward the grave are the same motion.

Cousin Hannah stands in the chapter as realism against Catherine's opium fantasy, insisting she is "spouseless" and bereft of love, and the two women divide again along the militant and dreamer seam the novel keeps drawing. Hannah is the "great captain" and "old warrior" who persists though there is "no defense, no answering cannon ball," a woman fighting systemic silence with a body that will not surrender; the "adamantine" mountains of wedlock are rigid and imprisoning, and her indomitable spirit outlasts them. Her strength, "like a finely tempered blade," "cold and nipping as the winter air," is an elemental femininity refusing mortal frailty, and Catherine both envies and is estranged from it, the complicated distance between women who have chosen different survivals.

The chapter deconstructs masculine authority as it goes, man reduced to "ephemeral" and a "broken sea shell," fragile and illusory beside the enduring strength of a woman like Hannah who has transcended "merely mortal needs" and "the idea of a man." Catherine's flirtations with imaginary lovers, her "magician" power to make and unmake reality, place female imagination as both refuge and trap. The chapter closes on marriage as the death of female autonomy and on two women, one militant and one dreaming, refusing that death from opposite ends of the same conviction.
woman-chapter-60:
Chapter 60

← Chapter 59 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 61 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Musician or gambler, the protagonist cannot say which he is, and the undecided self is this chapter's pillar. Music as transcendent and spiritual against the mundane obsession with gambling, the "elegiac mood" over slipping cards and decayed jockeys, is the fragility of a role and the fragility of identity itself, a self that will not settle into one calling. His ignorance of high society and finance, his indifference to whether "old ladies wear dresses of bone lace or bird-cages in paradise," carries the fading feminine decorum the book keeps noting, women defined by appearance and social ritual, and the "obituary columns" that "level" all classes and statuses are the dissolving of hierarchy the book welcomes, mortality the one force that unsorts what patriarchy sorts.

The moose call is the chapter's opening into another way of knowing. He calls and the moose answers, an "auditory hallucination" that crosses the line between natural and supernatural, and the answered call is voice and agency granted to a self outside societal roles, a recognition the ordinary world withholds. His limited musical knowledge set against the "basso profundo" of the moose and the "polysyllabic horns" of the wild ducks contrasts the formalized male-dominated art, the "musical composition," the "Stock Exchange" heard as a "long surf," with an untamed communal music, the non-hierarchical knowing the book keeps crediting to the feminine and the marginalized. His brother, dead and "confined to silence," marks the patriarchal limit, and the wild sounds are the diverse voices that resist classification the way the book's selves resist it.

The wild ducks give the chapter its crossing. He whispers to them and they respond, a "dialogic relationship" that defies patriarchal dominance and control, communication across the boundaries of species and worlds and states of being, and the crossing of those boundaries is the crossing point the book runs through gender, vulnerability and openness credited as strength rather than weakness. He stands still amid the chaos as a "fat gentleman," his stillness and trembling the precariousness and resilience of a marginalized self, and the lighthouse the birds dash against "as a star" is the danger that meets anyone seeking visibility and truth, the patriarchal gaze that blinds and destroys the ones drawn to its light.

The chapter ends attuned to the ducks as "exotic Pilgrims," "beautiful Asiatics," lightness and color and grace flying through "great clouds," and the fear of moving that keeps him still is the balance of presence and invisibility the book's women navigate, seen and unseen at once. His conclusion that his "elegy was this wild duck's horn" is the reclaiming of voice and narrative through connection with the natural and the marginalized, a music made outside the male tradition and the patriarchal record, an alternative legacy sounded on a wild horn where the composed elegy will not come. The undecided self finds its song not in the concert hall or the ledger but in the answered call of a creature that crosses every line the book means to dissolve.
woman-chapter-42:
Chapter 42

← Chapter 41 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 43 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer

The lost record is the chapter's pillar, and Young figures it as a fleet of vanished ships. Mr. Spitzer's obsession with lost voyages, ships gone "without trace," runs parallel to the feminist histories submerged beneath dominant narratives, the many suffrage campaigns and figures forgotten and their journeys unrecorded, and the effort to recover them is the effort to raise women's erased contributions from under the water. The mother's journey in a glass carriage with alabaster horses to visit the bedridden Cousin Hannah is solidarity among women across time and across the boundary of dying, a farewell that may exist "only in dreams" because feminist victories go unwitnessed and unvalidated.

Hannah's multiplicity holds the chapter's intersectional charge. Her disguises, "Arab king," suffrage captain, labor organizer, cross cultural and racial lines and register feminism's reach beyond gender alone, and the revelation of her secret love life breaks the stereotype of the asexual feminist warrior, restoring private desire and vulnerability to a public figure. The sacrifices her commitment demands, public duty set against personal fulfillment, are the costs the chapter refuses to hide even as it honors her.

Beneath the fading recognition runs the hidden feminine that endures. Hannah's "secretly feminine heart" beating "through all things" is the persistence of feminist strength under surfaces that deny it, influence surviving even where it goes unacknowledged. The death chamber veiled in desert tents, the east-west contrasts, situate her within feminism's global dimension, and Mr. Spitzer's role as male witness mediating her death marks how much feminist history reaches us through men who half-understand it. The chapter closes on death veiling all women as brides going to a bridegroom "cold as mountain snow," the "great mask of life" stripped to the human beneath, and the record still failing to hold what it should have kept.
woman-chapter-71:
Chapter 71

← Chapter 70 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 72 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Justice O’Leary · Tabitha · Vera Cartwheel

The doctor's office fills with births that never happen in this chapter, and the interrupted birth and invisibility carry it. Dr. O'Leary keeps instruments for delivery, a wooden arm, and a practice of imaginary pregnant patients, tending deliveries that produce nothing in a room where a "pregnant man" is rumored, and the phantom obstetrics is the empty pregnancy practice the book has run since Chapter 5, birth that will not complete presided over by a madman. The scattered, mateless women's shoes from many eras and places are the women who passed through this barren country and left only one shoe each, invisibility and erasure worked into a floor, and the wooden arm among the instruments is the body as the place the self comes apart set out among the tools of bringing a body into being.

Vera wears Catherine's pearls, the "real pearls" that cannot be lost or stolen, a lost estate carried on the body, and the pearls are women's dispossession and the failure of the record to hold a woman's inheritance folded into an ornament, the mother's fortune reduced to what a daughter can wear around her neck. Catherine's dream, even here, outfits a thief in aristocratic costume and promises to finance a revolution from her drugged bed, the woman's latent, unrealized power flickering under the stupor the world keeps her in.

O'Leary argues on with Sarah, the crawling silent woman he calls dead, and her toy drum and her muteness hold the boundary between life and death open around a dead child who will not leave, the same open threshold the book keeps for everyone it cannot let the world erase. The woman in metallic curlers who accuses Vera of being a "tramp girl," who curses the couples and denounces Jews and Communists and racial minorities, is a widow whose loneliness has curdled into the policing of other women, a female character both marginalized and reproducing the order that marginalizes her, and her half-dressed rage exposes the respectability she is failing to keep.

The landlord's wife, large and goitered, speaks her fragmented dialect of endurance, and Tabitha, the mute chambermaid who cares for the doctor, kneels washing the stone flaggings with her black curly head bowed, her whispered "Good-morning" a fragile assertion of presence. Tabitha is the unacknowledged female labor and the severed voice the book keeps honoring, invisibility and erasure carried by a woman who keeps the place running and is barely seen doing it, one more silent figure kept at the threshold where the book gathers the erased.
woman-chapter-80:
Chapter 80

← Chapter 79 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 81 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Esther Longtree · Walter

Walter is the one child who lived, and his living is this chapter's trouble. Esther bore him to a black father, a white woman's child across the line the town will not let her cross, and the personal tragedy of his birth and his "reproach" folds intersecting erasures of race and gender into a single figure, a son who accuses his mother and a mother who loves and grieves him at once. She tends him "in another country," and the distance is the emotional labor of a motherhood the world will not sanction, care performed across a separation the arrangement forces on her.

Esther is the mediator between the living and the dead, a "wet-nurse to the dead babies," and her perpetual pregnancy that flowers into loss is the interrupted birth held against the one child who survived it. The dead infants she nurses and the living son who accuses her occupy the same maternal ground, the dissolving boundary between life and death worked through a woman who mothers the vanished and the present in the same breath, kept at the threshold with all the book's dead.

Her paradox, that she "killed a child" and yet "the child lived," is the illusion of the individual at its most disturbing, a son who is both the murdered and the surviving, both accuser and beloved, and the child's voice as her conscience is the internalized weight of a motherhood judged by everyone. The lost inheritance, the old farm "erased," its fences changed until she cannot recognize them, is the failure of the record to hold a woman's lineage, her heritage and her reproductive history alike rubbed out.

Walter's conception, Esther "taken in the summer darkness," holds an ambiguity of consent the book refuses to resolve, vulnerability and survival and desire folded together in the dark. Her love endures past the town's rejection, and her ironic laughter about her child's race reclaims a complex, crossing motherhood the world would shame, whiteness and blackness held in one woman's arms. The chapter closes on her "everlasting pregnancy," the resilience of a body that goes on creating and losing and loving at the margin, a woman the arrangement cannot erase however hard it tries to unrecord her farm, her son, and her name.
woman-chapter-37:
Chapter 37

← Chapter 36 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 38 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer

Binaries dissolve everywhere in this chapter, and their collapse is the pillar. Heaven and hell, life and death, reality and dream run together; the question "Was he a domino or a man?" refuses to settle; every truth carries "a beautiful lie" and "each face hid the grinning skull." This is feminist skepticism toward the fixed positions patriarchy calls truth and it is the novel's own doctrine that "the individual is the one illusion," the two arriving as a single claim. Catherine's refusal to draw a clean line between illusion and reality, her acceptance of "the half of the earth which is always in darkness," is a way of knowing that rejects the male demand for one settled truth.

The dissolution goes all the way into gender and body. "Two forms were blended into one which was amorphous," "God was dog," men become women and women men, and the destabilizing of fixed gender is the plural selfhood the chapter prizes over any essential kind. Catherine's opium body, a "beautiful, bloated corpse," holds a rich inner life against its own inertia, the repression of a sedated woman and the sovereignty of a mind that will not be governed both true at once.

Cousin Hannah carries the transgression into the world. She infiltrates a sheik's harem, crosses cultural and gendered boundaries, and confounds the male authority that meets her, the sheik driven mad by her true face, so that female presence itself destabilizes patriarchal power. Her death and burial, her "undying strength," and Mr. Spitzer's felt "lack of grief" rather than grief, register the ambivalence around a woman's power in a world built to deny it. The chapter ends with Hannah's "fixed intensity" persisting past the loss of any object for it, the feminist spirit enduring even in defeat, and the binaries it broke staying broken.
woman-chapter-02:
Chapter 2

← Chapter 1 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 3 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer

Catherine's chapter is where the dissolution starts in earnest. Her sleep is "watchful, wide-eyed wakefulness," a state that is neither living nor dead, and the book will keep her there for the rest of its length. This is the dissolving boundary between life and death, and it is Catherine's permanent address, not a symbol of psychological imprisonment. Her bed dressed as a sarcophagus, her powdered birthmark, her belief in her own dual selves, one living and one dead, all say the same thing: she is the book's clearest case of a person held on both sides of the line at once.

Her opium world is the fullest statement so far of real and dream as one country. The imaginary guests, the phantoms, Pope and Byron, the invisible elephant she dares Mr. Spitzer to disprove: none is treated as error. They are a place, with its own weather and rules, and Catherine lives in it. And because the guests are all, finally, versions of her, the chapter is also plural selfhood. She has scattered herself across a houseful of visitors and cannot be found in any single one.

Mr. Spitzer enters here and his first scene is the first note of his own dissolution. Catherine accuses him of not existing, and the accusation is not a woman deflating a man; it is the book beginning to thin him out, the process that ends with him transparent. Even the canary matters. Spitzer secretly replaces each dead bird with a living one so the fiction holds. That is not a man managing a woman's life. It is the book keeping a dream stitched to the real until neither can be told from the other.
woman-chapter-24:
Chapter 24

← Chapter 23 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 25 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

The dream has taken the whole household by this chapter, not Catherine alone. The servants have gone into it to keep their places, the valet "waiting on Wellington," the gardener sure he is Potiphar's spouse, the Irish housemaid silent in company and speaking only to herself as a crowd of "fine ladies" and "fly-catching warblers." This is the servants' survival inside a mad house, and it is plural selfhood spread down through the staff, each of them scattered the way Catherine is scattered, the dream no longer one woman's but the building's, real and dream as one country with a full complement of dreamers.

They keep its rituals, arranging chrysanthemums for the dead, lighting fires for guests who never come, and Catherine at the center works the telephone, placing calls to the dead and the absent on a line that reaches only the servants' quarters. The calls that do not connect are the book's erasure, and the "horizontal lady" who must die inside her dreams to keep from waking into death is the life-and-death boundary held in a single sentence, a woman kept alive by staying dead to the world.

Mr. Spitzer is here too, unreliable, his image displaced by symbolic figures whenever Catherine reaches for him, a companion who cannot be counted on to be one thing or even one man.
