Vera, watching the chaos, weighs whom to bring her burning questions to and turns from Spitzer toward Miss MacIntosh, the grounded pole, though the reader now knows that pole is coming apart as surely as the rest.
woman-chapter-38:
Chapter 38

← Chapter 37 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 39 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah

Two modes of refusal share the chapter, and their doubling is the pillar. Cousin Hannah is the "great captain of extremes," the militant who sacrifices everything to suffrage and travels "to the outermost reaches of space"; Catherine is the "beautiful and unawakened corpse," the dreamer whose opium and romantic fantasy refuse the world from the opposite side. Action and dream are two faces of one unwillingness to accept a life the culture hands down, and Young holds them together without turning either into a simple lesson. Catherine's sense that suffrage is "quite unworthy" of Hannah's spirit is the ambivalence a dreamer feels toward the activist, and the gap between them is the gap between two feminist survivals rather than between courage and failure.

The chapter's deepest note is the burden of unexpressed love. Catherine's "dead love," never spoken and "as heavy as all the stars," names the erasure of women's emotional lives under an order that suppresses them, and it makes the unlived feeling weigh more than any lived one, restraint carrying a force the world never let it spend. Hannah's invitations to Egypt and far places, which Catherine cannot accept, are the missed openings for feminist awakening, and Catherine's imagined alternatives, riding "in balloons," picketing Buckingham Palace, wandering under nomadic stars, are the many shapes rebellion might have taken.

Hannah's strength stays elemental, "like a finely tempered blade," a "perpetual motion" that survives by fortitude and battles "one-eyed ogres greater than death," while Catherine's frailty and opium dreams are her own mode of endurance. The chapter closes on the confusion of truth and fantasy, the house as a "loony bin," dreams "more real than life," and it credits the dream as resistance even as it counts the cost of retreat. Action and dream rhyme, and the chapter leaves feminism as both a cause worth dying for and a haunted refuge.
woman-chapter-70:
Chapter 70

← Chapter 69 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 71 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Miss MacIntosh · Mrs. Hogden · Musidora Tidings

A corporeal woman intrudes on Catherine's dream in this chapter, and plural selfhood and the book's practice with the erased carry it. Mrs. Hogden arrives as a "faceless woman," a suspected shoplifter burdened with "worldly goods," layered in packages and eclectic objects, and the accumulation she carries is the cultural and material baggage the book keeps loading onto its women, a self buried under what it has gathered. Against Miss MacIntosh's practicality she is the disordered and chaotic woman, the other model of female existence, and the two of them, the disciplined and the cluttered, are two shapes the same constraint takes.

She insists on teaching arithmetic, imposing logic on a household ruled by dream, and her failure to be accepted by the bedridden Catherine makes her a "rival invalid," one aging, uncelebrated woman contending with another for standing in a house that has no room for either. Her eccentric solitude, the talking to herself, the chess played against invented partners with real tears at the wins and losses, is plural selfhood scattered across imagined company the way Catherine scatters herself across imaginary guests, a woman multiplying herself because the world has left her alone, and her weeping over a game humanizes her against every dismissal of the mad woman.

Her grotesque physicality, the neglect of hygiene, the refusal to be an invisible or attractive woman, is the book's confrontation with the unattractive figure the world erases, a body that will not disappear despite its flaws. Her delusion that she is mistress rather than servant, her invented social life, is the desire for the respect and power denied an aging, impoverished woman, and the servants who will not disillusion her grant her, quietly, the agency the house denies her outright, real and dream as one country extended down through the staff who let her keep her dream.

When she is removed at last by male legal authority, the removal is the patriarchal control over a woman's body and space made literal, a woman filed out of the house by the same machinery that files the wills. The playroom she leaves behind, full of discarded objects and traces, is the marginalized woman's history reduced to leavings, and the coded chalk message she writes on her way out is her small assertion of self against erasure, a self insisting on continuance where the record would keep nothing. The chapter leaves her the way the book leaves all its erased, present and unaccounted for, gone from the house and not gone from it, kept at the threshold with Musidora and the coachman and Martha and the mute, one more woman the arrangement could not quite make disappear.
woman-chapter-23:
Chapter 23

← Chapter 22 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 24 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Miss MacIntosh mounts a long argument against the electric light in this chapter, and the argument keeps arriving at the crossing point. In the old dark, she says, "a man had married a man, and a woman had married a woman, and no one had been the wiser." This is a complaint about the exposure modern life forces on people, and it is her own account of the seam the book writes from: darkness let the categories blur, and the blurring hurt no one, and the light that sorts them again is the loss. She is defending, in her plain practical voice, the very dissolution she believes she stands against.

Her scorn for Franklin and Edison "meddling with creation," breaking the given rhythm of day and night, is her resistance to male hubris, and it is the book's suspended time, a woman who wants the hours left as they were, who "could never remember having dreamed even her own dreams" and keeps a strict, unsleeping consciousness against the whole apparatus of change. The heart, she says, is "locked from the inside," which is the unknowable self stated as fact, plural selfhood in a sentence.

She refuses the "filmy dress" and the "white rose," and she looks toward winter and the "two igloos" that will hold her and Vera at the roof of the world. The light she trusts is the stars', not the wire's, the natural illumination against the manufactured, the dark she keeps defending because it is where people were allowed to stop being sorted.
woman-chapter-13:
Chapter 13

← Chapter 12 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 14 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Vera crosses a frozen lake without knowing the depth beneath it, and the image is the chapter's method: a surface walked in confidence over a dissolving deep. What she learns, saying goodbye to Miss MacIntosh, is that the woman she washed and ironed for was "the strangest being on earth" and was never known at all, plural selfhood in the character the book keeps building to look most single.

The gardens of the dream open around her. Dr. Galen and Dr. Harvey stand among the guests, the dead present with the living, and the air is full of "wheeling skirts" and "masks" and a chessboard whose squares move under life-sized chessmen. The masks and the moving board are the self as mask and the dreamed world made solid, real and dream as one country. Venus stands "bearded by patriarchal fog," and the bearded Venus is the crossing point in a single image, the female figure with a grown beard, gender coming apart where the reader can watch it happen.

The chapter closes in the "garden of the deaf," where "the ear is dead" and Catherine insists that neither she nor Mr. Spitzer can hear or be heard. A frog screams and no one hears it. "One should see," the passage says, "but one should not hear the song." This is the silencing of women, and it is the book's deepest statement so far of invisibility and erasure, a whole garden built around a severed sense, where silence itself becomes the music, and the unheard song is the one the book keeps playing for anyone deaf to it.
woman-chapter-49:
Chapter 49

← Chapter 48 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 50 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Joachim Spitzer

Ice encases the world in this chapter, and the frozen field is where its erasures are kept. Mr. Spitzer is disoriented in a watery grave, walking "on frozen waters without wetting his feet," a "starfish on his sleeve" and barnacles on his cheek, and the recurring star is "honed away" over "many hidden depths" and "many whirlpools." This is the submerged history of women held under the ice and the dissolving boundary between life and death, a man neither drowned nor dry crossing a surface with everything lost beneath it. The "beautiful ladies" frozen into "ancient patriarchs" return, the crossing point set in ice again, and the drowned cities are the erased that the book keeps rather than releases.

Martha the passenger pigeon carries the chapter's grief, and she carries it as a woman erased. The last of her kind, she died "without confessing her pigeon peccadilloes," relegated to the baggage car, mourned only in the "whispered murmurs" of an old black porter, and the caretaker dismisses her soul as "not so much as a bubble of light," insisting "two passenger pigeons would be two more than there were." This is female extinction and reproductive futility and the intersecting erasures of race, and it is the book's practice with the vanished: Mr. Spitzer becomes the "old pigeon lobbyist," the advocate for "lost causes," the one who keeps the extinct present the way he keeps every threshold open. The impossibility of reviving the species "even upon some other star" holds the loss where the book will not let it close.

Mr. Spitzer's own dissolution runs alongside Martha's. He is the "pleader of lost causes," the "minority representing a majority," the "barcarolle heard not by the singer," his tears enclosing "suns, moons, flowers, butterflies," and "none mourned for him." The self with no single account of itself and the music that goes unheard arrive together, a man who winds himself "like an old clock" and cannot say whether he is a "rain drop falling from the wing of the great archangel Uriel" or a tear. His body is an "old, many-chimneyed tenement," his rounds a "watchman" and a "beagle" knocking on "frozen doorbells," and the knocking that no one answers is invisibility worked into a nightly ritual.

The chapter's deepest trust is given to those who have lost a sense. Mr. Spitzer relies on the deaf musician and the blind lighthouse keeper, on people "who had forgotten their origins," and the severed sense that the book uses for erasure becomes, here, an alternative way of knowing, sight and hearing set aside as the only paths to truth. Time thins to "signs of this moment only," the past and future fluid, and the self multiplies into a "living lighthouse" and a "weaver" caught in the storm, images doubling until self cannot meet self. The chapter closes on crowds and alienation, voices "like all dead souls returning," "pigeon murmurs" and "heart murmurs" running together, and music "coming when his heart should beat no more," the unheard song sounding past the death of the one who makes it, and the truth left unknowable and accepted as such.
woman-chapter-58:
Chapter 58

← Chapter 57 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 59 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer

An old violinist plays music no one can hear in this chapter, and the unheard song is its pillar. Frail and ghostly, with a "wounded chin" and "no buttons on his shirt," he draws his bow across silence, and Mr. Spitzer perceives the music with full technical and emotional understanding, so that the invisibility of the unheard performance and the marginalized life it stands for arrive together, a man playing to a world that cannot hear him. The music evokes "the beating of his mother's heart," a "minor composition" that would be "less beautiful if heard by living ears," and the maternal heartbeat carries motherhood and the ephemeral, undervalued feminine experience the book keeps recovering, the "shadings of thought and unconscious memory" that belong to a realm the dominant order dismisses.

The music frees Mr. Spitzer from "corporeal woes," a detachment from the body that is the body as the place the self comes apart eased for a moment into flight, and its ethereal weather, "bird calls," "whispering rain," "sea shells buzzing like bees," is the feminine principle of connection to the organic and cyclical. The violinist shaking "like an aspen tree," "bare branches filled with singing birds," is feminized by the delicacy of the imagery, and Mr. Spitzer's dreaming of other lives for him, ball-player and gentleman and shepherd and judge and fisherman and king, is the plural selfhood the book distributes across everyone, the many masculine roles a self could wear tried on over a ragged coat that fits none of them. The "if only" his bow were another instrument names the limitation society imposes, the potential the world will not let a marginal life realize.

Reality goes "fugitive," "just so many sticks," a "pole or wand or staff or rod," and the arbitrariness of the symbols is the book's refusal of fixed and essential kinds, gendered emblems shown to be interchangeable objects. Mr. Spitzer's obsession with his brother anchors his understanding in a male figure while women stay absent, the patriarchal orientation of memory, and the "old fighters" and "old runners" "broken by life," the athletes he attends to only after Peron's death, are masculinity revealed as vulnerable and aging and mortal, the heroic ideal undone. The boundaries blur between living and dead, music and silence, real and dream, and the violinist's "wire-drawn body," his "mad puppet" movements, a "creature spewed up from the infernal depths," are a self with its agency gone, moved by strings it does not hold.

Mr. Spitzer cannot say whether the musician is "dead" or "dreaming," and the not-knowing is the boundary between life and death held open on a single body. The music "existing only in Mr. Spitzer's imagination," the hesitation to break the silence with applause, is the silencing of the unheard voice and the reverence the book pays it, and the violinist "whirling like a singing top dying down," the "recording angel" with "snow-white pinions," is the invisible labor of creation, the work that goes unwitnessed the way women's work does. Mr. Spitzer as a "walking score board" or abacus is the keeper of accounts the book keeps feminizing, and the music "not even for the white keyboard," "existing apart from transitory sound," is the non-dominant expression that defies the categories entirely. The chapter closes with his "black cape whirling," a "cord drifting like a bellrope," the protective darkness around him, and the ambiguity of whether the musician or the music or the man himself exists at all, the unheard song still sounding inside a mind that cannot tell its own presence from its absence.
woman-chapter-81:
Chapter 81

← Chapter 80 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 82 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Esther Longtree

Esther chooses a "legal father" for her child in this chapter, and the crossing point runs through the choosing. The "little toy salesman" she selects is small and childlike, "drinking milk from a baby bottle," unable to "tie his own shoe-laces," and the man infantilized against Esther's swelling dominance is the crossing point in the roles themselves, the woman grown large and strong where the man is reduced to an infant, the seam the book writes from opened in a marriage where the wife protects and teaches the husband. She is the "swollen bride of a little man," and the inversion turns the whole patriarchal arrangement over, female power set against a masculinity shrunk to dependence.

His body is its own coming-apart, a "large head," a "puffy body," a "waddling gait" set against a "powerful" and "pugnacious" upper half, an incomplete manhood the book keeps deflating. His survival of a shipwreck in which all the others drowned, "the women, the children, the moon, the sun, the stars," is male entitlement to survival named without mercy, a man who lived at the expense of everyone the sea took, and his "murderer" status is the guilt of that uneven survival, the burden the book keeps placing on those who outlast the drowned.

His psychological and physical deterioration, his "black mourning band" and "dead rosebud," his haunted memory of the drowned, are the trauma the book grants even its diminished men, and the "dead child's hand" clinging to him is the same spectral weight Esther carries, the lost child present at the threshold across two bodies. His stunted development set against Esther's "everlasting pregnancy" is the interrupted birth doubled, a man who never grew and a woman who never delivers, two arrested lives bound in a marriage neither the world nor the book will let complete.

Esther plans to "teach him" proper behavior, to make of this infant husband a father, and her hope for marriage and legitimacy is a woman reaching for the sanction the world withholds even as she inverts its terms. The looming war, the destruction and loneliness ahead, and her thought that "maybe the dead loved the dead" fold the boundary between life and death into her future the way it has folded into her past, and the chapter closes on Esther as a "pregnant old mule," the burden and the strength of a female endurance that carries dreams and lost children through a hostile world, still creating, still unfinished, still at the threshold the book keeps for its own.
woman-chapter-52:
Chapter 52

← Chapter 51 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 53 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Joachim Spitzer

Veils and masks open this chapter, and the ambiguity they hold is its pillar. The old suffragette's identity and losses are shrouded, a "sea shell born without a mantle," a "brook without water," and the feminism of absence and yearning and the self that cannot be fixed arrive together, a woman defined by what is missing from her. Mr. Spitzer cannot say whether she was mother or father to him, source of "amputated loves," and his thought that "perhaps she should be the husband and not the bride" is the crossing point stated plainly, the categories of the marriage rite dissolving on the woman who would not enter it.

Mr. Spitzer is a "pawnbroker who had pawned himself," a "locksmith in a street of dreams where there was neither key nor lock," "dominoes of which there were no spots," "no name, no face," and the alienation of the marginalized and the self dissolving toward blankness are one figure, a man who has hocked himself into the vanished trades and old crafts the suffragette is merged with. The "mother-of-pearl paved court" and the "veiled dancing girls" carry the objectification and veiling of women, literal and figurative, into the same dream.

The suffragette's fluidity is the chapter's engine. She is "indifferent to the election," howling in a snowstorm, her "lost skirt" the lost femininity or autonomy the skirt both grants and confines, her multilingual cries of "Long live woman!" carrying feminism across every border. She dresses as a man, climbs "old mountains as if they were new" with practical gear, and may be "the bridegroom to her bride," the crossing point again destabilizing the marriage rite and the fixed self. Her adventures, challenging prime ministers, sleeping among Laplanders, flying over the Alps, make her an iconoclast and a "lost star," a "black knight," and the Swiss fear of her "disrupting mountains and skies," the "blackamoor" nickname, carry feminism's disruptive force and its intersection with race and the exotic into the myth.

Trunks and locked boxes hold the chapter's last figures, "bridal gowns and veils" behind keys, feminist archives hidden and inaccessible, a "multiplicity of bridal gowns without slippers" marking a marriage refused or unrealized. She is a "type of the uncreated creation," a woman who "achieves without love and loves without realization," and the paradox is the illusion of the individual at the edge of being, a self that is and is not, present and absent, bride and bridegroom. Whether she was "male or female" the chapter will not say, and it closes with her reading an old romance of unattainable lovers and pennies laid on her eyelids, the crossing point and the mystery held to the last, a life the record could not sort and the book will not pretend to.
woman-chapter-65:
Chapter 65

← Chapter 64 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 66 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Lorena · Miss MacIntosh · Mr. Titus Bonebreaker

Mr. Bonebreaker preaches at Miss MacIntosh through this chapter, and the body coming apart and the unmasking that follows carry it. He is the Gospel salesman who casts himself as her spiritual rescuer, demanding she give up "carnal lusts" and worldly ambition, and his controlling religiosity is the paternalistic salvation the book keeps setting against female autonomy, a man who would save a woman by governing her. Her wounds, the amputated breast and the baldness, are the body as the place the self comes apart, and her decision to show them to him before the marriage, to reveal the bald head and the scarred side rather than let the wig lie, is the unmasking made an act of honesty, the self stripped of its cover offered as the truth it is.

He flees the sight of her, and the umbrella goes with him, and the flight is the failure of male authority to accept the real woman under the mask, the man who preached salvation unable to look at what salvation would have to love. Miss MacIntosh rejects his God and his way of life after, and the rejection is her refusal of the whole apparatus that would sort her into shame, the same refusal she brings to jewels and empire and illusion.

The wigs she wears in different places and times, black in memory of Lorena and red in memory of her brother, are the self as mask worn in colors that hold her dead, plural selfhood carried on the head, and the Chinatown where she learns solitaire and finds hairlessness admired inverts the beauty standard the West wraps around her. The solitaire she plays alone, wishing for a "watcher" to see that no one cheats even against an invisible opponent, is a woman keeping vigil over a fairness the world will not keep for her.

She works among the blind and is content there, among people who cannot see her difference, and the blind who cannot see her baldness are invisibility and erasure turned for once into shelter, the severed sense that the book uses for erasure become a place a marginalized woman can be whole. Her drift toward seeking her lost brother among Polynesian head-hunters carries the head motif to the far side of the world, and the honeymooners' hotel where she registers as a single woman, alone among couples, is the social order that has no room for her name without a raised voice. The chapter leaves her standing apart on the water while Mr. Bonebreaker's voice booms invisibly over it, erased and enduring at once, the woman the arrangement cannot place and cannot quite make disappear.
woman-chapter-59:
Chapter 59

← Chapter 58 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 60 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Joachim Spitzer

Forlorn musicians fill the street at the start of this chapter, and Mr. Spitzer's alms to them open its pillar: the self as borrowed flesh, a body worn rather than owned. His indiscriminate generosity, and the caution he learns because a beggar may be a king and a king a beggar, is the instability of social status the book keeps exposing and the negotiation with appearance that pins the marginalized, the surface hiding whatever it likes underneath. From there the chapter turns metaphysical, and Mr. Spitzer's alienation from his own body, his sense of being "another" or "not himself," is the constructed, performed self, the masks and cloaks and borrowed flesh that make identity a costume the way gender is a costume.

His fear of losing identity, of thresholds, of silence, is the fear of erasure the book knows women by, and the sound and music that are "ephemeral" and easily lost are the silencing of the unheard voice, silence held as both a loss and a site of power. Mr. Spitzer as a "psychological beggar" and "clown" is the reductive role the book keeps forcing on the marginalized, the "madwoman" or "fool" a person is flattened into, and the deceptive appearances and the "revolving door" are the cyclical entrapment and the charitable paternalism the book meets with suspicion, aid dispensed without touching the system that made the need.

Death and transformation dissolve the chapter's boundaries. Mr. Spitzer as a "cloud" or "shadow," alienated from his own skeleton, is the body as the place the self comes apart, and the "temporary tenant" who does not own the flesh he lives in is the objectified body the book keeps taking from its women and handing, here, to a man, a self renting a skeleton that is not his. The "unholy trinity" of body and soul and spirit as mutable, the fear of losing identity, the thought of having "begotten himself" without human love, is plural selfhood reaching toward the interrupted birth, a creation with no parent and no consummation.

The chapter ends on his admission that he is "already dead," caught in equivocation and ambiguous existence, and the liminal state between life and death is invisibility and erasure worked to its limit on the witness, a man neither present nor absent who names his own condition and cannot resolve it. Though the chapter follows a man, its whole apparatus, the borrowed flesh, the invaded body, the silence that is both erasure and refuge, the self as costume, is the equipment the book built for its women, and Mr. Spitzer inhabits it the way the book means everyone finally to inhabit it, dispossessed of any single, owned self.

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Two kinds of clocks run in this chapter. Old Reliable, which Miss MacIntosh winds by hand, keeps the ordinary hours of order and discipline. Around it stand the frozen enchanted clocks, stopped, holding their single moments forever. This is the halting of oppressive social time, and it is suspended time, the two clocks running at once, one measuring the day and one refusing to, in the same house.

Vera slips out into the night, past the "veil of oblivion," toward the "faces pulsing in the vacancy" and the statues poised between sleep and waking, and the passage is the real and the dream as one country, the ordinary house opening onto a dreamed one without a seam. At its center is the "garden of the blind," made by touch and scent for Vera's grandmother, who could not see. It is the alternative perception granted a marginalized woman, and it is the book's motif of the severed sense, invisibility and erasure worked into a garden, the same thread as the deaf villagers and the blindness the book keeps returning to.

The chapter dwells on eyelashes and eyebrows and hair, on Absalom's hair and on the Mona Lisa's missing eyebrows, which it says add "beauty to the mystery." These are the protective features of a face, and they are the body's removable parts, the body as the place the self comes apart, and the missing eyebrows point straight ahead to Miss MacIntosh, whose own are gone. Miss MacIntosh anchors the chapter as the pole that restores Vera from "childhood madness" and dismisses the visions, her face "bristling with needles and pins," guarded like armor. Against her, Vera's mother senses that Mr. Spitzer is not entirely "substantial," a self growing thin and fluid, which reaches past gender toward the same bottom the women are finding.
woman-chapter-82:
Chapter 82

← Chapter 81 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Woman's Experiences →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Esther Longtree · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Peron Spitzer · Vera Cartwheel

The book ends with Vera unable to confess her losses to Esther, and the illusion of the individual and the dissolving boundary between life and death close it together. She loves "an older love than memory" and mourns "three deaths," and the losses she cannot share, the mother, the ancestral home, the guide, are the grief the book has run on since its first page, a mourning with no bottom and no witness. Her long meditation on the deaf and the blind, the ear that is "dead," is invisibility and erasure gathered for the last time, the severed sense the book has used from the deaf villagers of Chapter 4 to the mute of Chapter 61, women and marginal figures cut off and unheard.

Catherine dies at last, a "beautiful lady sleeping in her swan boat," walking "as if through water" on Mr. Spitzer's arm, and her death is the boundary between life and death the book held open for her since Chapter 2 finally, quietly closing. Mr. Spitzer confesses that he is Peron and not Joachim, that his love for Catherine was hidden all along, and the confession collapses the two brothers the book kept doubling into one man, the "old bride" and the "old bridegroom," the crossing point and the illusion of the individual resolved in a single figure who was never quite two and never quite one.

The storm takes Catherine's property and the house with it, the golden turrets swept into the sea, and the old clam-digger, Spitzer's valet, disappears into the sand, mourned by Mr. Spitzer more than Catherine is, the marginal figure valued at last as the book values all its erased. The clam-digger buried in sand, present and unaccounted for, is the book's practice with the erased performed one final time, the vanished kept at the threshold, and the question of whether physical survival without vitality is survival at all is the book's own question about what it means to be kept and not quite alive.

Esther appears again in her old waterproof, unable to swim, rejecting Vera's illusions about the sea, and her groundedness against Vera's mysticism is the practical woman set against the dreaming one, the two modes the book has run in parallel from Miss MacIntosh to Catherine. In the next room a man addresses a "silent woman," insisting that "Man loves a silent woman," and his loudness against her silence is the silencing of women stated plainly at the book's end, the enforced quiet the whole novel has been listening past, the unheard song still playing for anyone deaf to it.

The man Vera comes to love is stone deaf, hearing "through his eyes and his fingers," awakened to a silent world he fills with an inner life, and his alternative way of knowing is the book crediting the severed sense as a mode of perception rather than only a wound, the deaf man who hears what the hearing cannot. His recognition of shared suffering across race and gender, Vera's vision of lost pearls and clouds merging earth and sky, of marriage and community and love shared with nature and human beings, gather the illusion of the individual into its final affirmation, every heart the other heart made not a loss now but a belonging. Esther Longtree closes the book as the "mother of the stillborn," her handwritten note misspelled and human, "Owt to luntsch. bee bak in a whale," the erased woman leaving her mark on the record at last, imperfect and present, and the novel ends where it began, in a country where the living and the dead, the real and the dreamed, the self and the other are one, and every woman it kept at the threshold is still there, still enduring, still refusing to disappear.

Characters: Miss MacIntosh

The wig lies on the floor of this chapter "like a rare tropical bird," a self shed and left where it fell. Around it is the plain inventory of Miss MacIntosh's room, the knitting needles and sewing baskets and soapstone dishes, the patched clothes, the bust of Martin Luther, the cheesecloth thrown over the broken cherubim. This is female domestic labor and survival, and it is the surface the book has laid over the dissolution all along, the material the real kept scrupulously in order above a woman who is coming apart underneath it.

She sleeps bald, without eyebrows or eyelashes, and the chapter ends on the amputated breast, "no bigger than a baby's," the body as the place the self comes apart shown at last without the wig or the corset to soften it. The playing cards near her, the deuce of clubs read as "the test of tears" and "the omen of death," hold the life-and-death boundary in a card, and her refusal to be a "weathercock" or a "turncoat" is the grounded woman's last stand against a world that will not stay fixed.

The room itself has begun to give way to the sea. The door is barred but crusted with seaweed and barnacles, sea boots stand ready, the umbrella lies open on the floor. The woman who keeps clear of the "greatest waves" has the ocean growing on her own door, the real and the dream as one country closing in on the one character built to keep them apart.

Chapter 4

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · The Stone Deaf Man · Vera Cartwheel

Grief is the engine of this chapter, and it is grief of the permanent kind. Vera has been haunted for years, declining, keeping a fire lit on the shore as a signal to a woman who does not come. The mourning does not lessen and does not resolve into anything, which is the pillar exactly: not an event with an end but a standing condition. Around this, Catherine decrees that Vera must accept a "death in the midst of life," and the phrase is not, at bottom, about the silencing of a daughter. It is the dissolving boundary between life and death handed down as an instruction, a living death Vera is told to inhabit.

The dead girl's letters carry the chapter's sharpest figure. She had accepted marriage proposals from a series of interchangeable strangers, then jumped from the Brooklyn Bridge with her suitcase and veil. The interchangeable men are commodification and are also the illusion of the individual seen from its bleakest side: the strangers are not distinct, they blur into one another, and the girl's death is one more open threshold. She is a double of Vera, a version of the path not taken, plural selfhood reaching across two women who are versions of each other.

The deaf old people at the chapter's edge are not a footnote about society refusing to hear women. They are the first appearance of a motif the book returns to for the rest of its length, invisibility and erasure through the cutting-off of a sense, the world going silent, which comes back in the garden of the deaf and the stone deaf man Vera comes to love.

Chapter 28

← Chapter 27 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 29 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer

Metamorphosis is the pillar of this chapter, and Young routes it through Catherine's narcotic mind and Mr. Spitzer's butterflies. Catherine's dreams throw up "Russian bishops, queens, duchesses, birds, and serpents," a feminine interior that is at once richly generative and drugged into passivity, so that the same visionary power which makes her a maker of worlds also holds her still. Her "obtuse faith" in Mr. Spitzer's return is maternal persistence, the woman who keeps life and memory going while incapacitated, and the chapter treats that persistence as a real force rather than a symptom.

The butterflies carry the metamorphosis outright. Delicate, ephemeral, transforming, they are the feminized emblem of renewal, and Mr. Spitzer's patient devotion to them is a mode of knowing that runs against his brother Peron's engagement with "the cruelty of actual life." Contemplative aesthetic attention sits on one side and brute pragmatism on the other, feminine and masculine by the old coding, and Young's sympathy stays with the butterflies. When Peron dies and Mr. Spitzer abandons the collecting, the abandonment reads as the way a patriarchal reality suppresses the feminine, spiritual attention it cannot use.

The return to Catherine's "enchanted" room, its "ethereal gleamings" and "semi-faces," is the return of a masculine wanderer to a feminine source, and it names interiority and liminality as sites of both power and vulnerability. The butterfly's indistinguishable beginning and end, birth folded into death, gives the chapter its final figure: cyclical time against the straight line, the interconnection of living and dying that patriarchal chronology cannot admit. Mr. Spitzer's "sporadic butterfly memories" are his intermittent access to that cycle, and the chapter keeps the feminine principle, generative, transformative, resilient, at its center even as it follows a man contemplating wings.

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel

Catherine's dream fills this chapter with guests, and the guests are all, at bottom, versions of her. The Queen Maud Mountains arrive as an imperious, aloof woman holding a parasol, and the face the parasol conceals is Catherine's own. The reflections in her crowded musical evenings have no faces. Rameses fragments into several selves before her. This is the feminized geography and the powerful, inaccessible woman, and it is plural selfhood, Catherine scattered so far across her visitors that she can be found in a mountain range and a pharaoh and a stranger's reflection but not in any single self called Catherine.

The dream is treated as a place with duties. Catherine frets as a "great hostess" over whether there are "not enough pyramid-shaped ices," and the fret is not comic relief. It is the labor of holding a whole country together, real and dream as one country, kept furnished and lit by a woman who lives nowhere else. Her guests are drawn from every era and are separated from one another by time, space, and death, and none of that keeps them from her table.

Catherine herself is trapped between life and death, and the chapter keeps her there. Sir Walter Raleigh's atheist propositions about God are welcome in the dream beside the pharaohs and the knights, because the dream admits everything and sorts nothing. The reflections without faces are the illusion of the individual seen from inside a mind that is dissolving: a room full of selves, not one of them separable, not one of them whole.
woman-the-route-down:
The Route Down

← Why a second edition · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 1 →

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Esther Longtree · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh

What this book is offering

Radical Immanence is a name this edition brings to Miss MacIntosh, My Darling. It is not a name Marguerite Young used. I believe she incorporated a complete philosophical system in her novel, but I do not know if she said this bluntly to anyone. Young did not call herself a feminist, and she did not claim that any system of thought stood behind the book.

Radical Immanence is a contemporary vocabulary, a set of reading tools, offered for what the novel already enacts. The claim is not that Young studied a theory and then dramatized it. The claim runs the other way. The novel arrived at these structures through fiction, working them out sentence by sentence across the eighteen years of its writing, before the language for describing them had settled. Naming them now does not smuggle a later philosophy back into an earlier book. It gives a reader words for what the book was doing all along.

That order matters, because the first objection to a reading like this one is that it is anachronistic, that it dresses an earlier novel in the clothes of a later theory. The answer is to grant the timing and deny the direction. The theory came later. The structures came first, in the novel, made of image and scene rather than argument.

A word on the term itself, since this book leans on it. Immanence, stripped of its usual heaviness, means that meaning lives inside experience rather than above it. There is no vantage point outside the world from which things can be sorted and judged in a clean way. Radical Immanence, as a way of reading, holds that the novel refuses any such outside position. Inside the book there is no stable floor from which to separate the real from the dreamed, the living from the dead, the single self from the many selves it scatters into. Everything happens inside consciousness, and consciousness, followed far enough, has no fixed categories at the bottom.

The Thesis

Here is the claim the rest of this book rests on.

Young goes so far down into consciousness that the categories a reader brings to the book stop holding.

Living and dead, waking and dreaming, man and woman, one self and the crowd of selves inside it: each comes apart under the pressure of how far the novel is willing to go. The book does not argue that these distinctions are false. It dissolves them by description, by staying inside a mind until the lines a reader counted on go soft.

Women are where the book goes in. This is the part most easily misread. The claim is not that Miss MacIntosh, My Darling is, in the end, a book about women. The claim is that women are the route. The women in the novel already have their selfhood broken open by the conditions of their lives.

Catherine, sealed in her opium dreams, has already scattered into a house full of guests who are all versions of her.

Esther, pregnant forever and delivering nothing, already lives at the place where creation and loss are the same event.

Miss MacIntosh, bald under her red wig and missing a breast, already wears her identity as something removable.

These are not women whose wholeness the book must break open. They arrive already broken open, and that openness is the door. The route runs through them toward something that has no gender at the bottom.

This is where the male figures matter, and why this edition puts one of them forward early. Mr. Spitzer cannot tell which brother he is. He stands as the bride at a wedding while a woman stands as the groom. He is called dead while he goes on walking, and late in the book he thins out almost to transparency. If the dissolving of the self were only a fact about the women in the novel, Spitzer would be a problem, a run of chapters to apologize for. He is not a problem. He is the proof. What the women reach through their conditions, he reaches too.

The bottom of consciousness, in this book, has no sex.

The conversation this reading joins

This is not the first time readers have noticed that the novel dissolves things. The reading here builds on work that saw the pattern and named parts of it, and it should be taken as company rather than as a wall of defense.

Miriam Fuchs, in "Liquescence as Form," read the novel's very form as a kind of melting. In her account the book does not hold its shapes still. Character, scene, and identity run together, and that flowing is not a loss of control but the form itself, the thing the book is built to do. This edition takes that insight about form and carries it into content. What melts, finally, is not only the shape of the prose but the categories the prose is made of, gender among them.

Steven Shaviro, in "Lost Chords and Interrupted Births," fixes on the motif of the birth that never completes, the pregnancy that will not deliver, the note that will not resolve. Esther Longtree is the clearest case, carrying and carrying and bringing nothing to term. Shaviro saw in that interruption something central to how the book works. This edition reads the interrupted birth as one of the pillars named below, the state in which the unfinished is not a failure but a way of being, and it follows that state past Esther into the whole novel.

Behind both essays stands the recovery work of Breaking the Sequence, which placed Young where she belongs, among the women experimentalists whose books had been pushed to the edge of the record. That placement did the first necessary thing. It said the novel was serious, and it said whose company it kept.

What this edition adds is not a correction of that work but a longer reach through it. The essays saw the dissolution and named its parts. This book follows the dissolution all the way down and gives it one account:

Young uses women as the route into consciousness, and going deep enough dissolves the category of gender itself.

The reading is offered as an extension of a conversation already underway, not as a claim to have started it.

The eleven pillars, briefly

The chapters that follow read the novel through eleven pillars. They are reading tools, not doctrine, and they are meant to be used and set down, not believed. Each is easiest to hold if it is attached to a character:

Plural selfhood: the "I" that is many. Catherine, scattered across the guests of her dream.

The crossing point: the place where man and woman trade. The wedding where Mr. Spitzer is the bride and Miss MacIntosh the groom, and the "secret man" the book finds inside women.

Unfinished is not failed: incomplete as a way of being. Esther, pregnant and never delivering.

Permanent grief: mourning with no end. Esther again, at her stillbirths.

The dissolving boundary between life and death: Catherine, living and dead in the same breath.

The real and the dream are one country: Catherine's opium world, treated as a place and not an error.

The body as the place the self comes apart: Miss MacIntosh, her baldness and her missing breast.

The illusion of the individual: the novel's own line, "Every heart is the other heart. Every soul is the other soul. The individual is the one illusion."

The self as mask: Miss MacIntosh's wig, worn and removed; Mr. Spitzer, clothed by another hand.

Suspended time: Catherine's stopped clocks, running and frozen at once.

Invisibility and erasure: Mr. Spitzer thinned to transparency, and Martha, the last passenger pigeon, mourned by a man who cannot save her.

Spitzer stands under several of these on purpose. He is the reminder, kept in view, that the frame reaches past gender.

The Crossing Point

Speaking to Friedman and Fuchs, she said: "I never thought of myself as either a woman or a man. I thought of myself as a person who was born to be a writer, who was doomed to be a writer."

Young wrote from the crossing point. She did not stand on one side of the line between man and woman and look across it. She wrote from the seam, from the place where the categories give way, which is exactly the place her characters keep finding. The line about being neither woman nor man is not Young declining to be political. It is Young naming where she wrote from.

Young went on: "there have been men who have seemed to want to destroy me or my writing, men I don't even know. …I think there is a rage against women. I've come to see that now although at the time I did not notice it." The two statements are usually treated as if they pull against each other, the refusal of gender on one side and the naming of misogyny on the other.

They do not pull against each other.

They are cause and result.

A writer who refuses the category the culture insists on does not escape the category. She draws its rage. The woman who says she is neither woman nor man, only a writer, and who then writes eighty-two chapters from the place where that distinction dissolves, is met by exactly the fury a culture keeps for those who will not stay sorted. The refusal and the rage belong to one story.

What this book asks

The book asks the reader to entertain the idea that the dissolving of fixed categories in Miss MacIntosh, My Darling is not a flaw to be excused, not a difficulty to be managed, and not a private feminine mysticism, but the deliberate deep work of the novel, reached through women and carried past them. A reader can grant that much and still argue with any single reading in the chapters that follow. The pillars are tools, and tools can be picked up or set down. But the premise, that Young went down into consciousness until the categories dissolved and wrote from that depth, is the ground the rest of this edition stands on. It is offered here in the plainest terms it can be given, so that a skeptical reader can finish this and grant the premise while keeping every right to resist the conclusions.

Chapter 73

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Esther Longtree · Joe Goldberg

The dying fathers write to Esther in this chapter, and the failure of the record to hold a woman's experience runs beneath the interrupted birth. As each man nears death he seeks assurance about the child she never brought to term, and Esther's silence in answer is protective and it is the book's erasure turned into a woman's own strategy, a mute refusal to hand these men a comfort the truth cannot give. She thinks of sending them tangible proof, a hand or a foot, and the impossibility of the gesture, the child reduced to a fragment that could be mailed, is the interrupted birth at its bleakest, motherhood proven by a piece.

The old doctor advises her to keep silent to protect male vanity, and the counsel names the whole arrangement, a woman's truth suppressed so a man's story can stand, and Esther cannot recall the father of the "little shadow boxer" or the champion featherweight at all. The forgetting is the failure of the record run backward, the man's memory dominating while the woman's experience blurs, and her solitude is the loneliness of a body that carries what no one will witness.

Joe Goldberg, the dying featherweight champion, writes to her full of nostalgia and regret, wanting a legacy through the child, and his fading strength beside Esther's endurance sets male physical triumph against male frailty, the fighter undone while the woman goes on. The graveyard where she remembers him, the encounter shrouded in violation and half-memory, is the dissolving boundary between life and death that Esther lives on, intimacy and trauma and the dead all folded into one ground she cannot fully recover.

The old mule, barren and mournful, stands for the sterility the town pins on her, and the "birth of nothing" she suffers again is the interrupted birth in its purest form, labor without a child, agony with no arrival. The white feather drifting at the chapter's close is loss and ambiguous hope at once, and Esther nurses her own fist among the lost children, a woman whose motherhood is real and unwitnessed, kept at the threshold the book reserves for everyone it will not let the world forget.
woman-chapter-78:
Chapter 78

← Chapter 77 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 79 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Esther Longtree · Rosemary

"Little Jackass" is the name Esther carries from birth in this chapter, given for her stubbornness and her unwillingness to be born, and the resistance is a girl's refusal of the roles set for her before she has drawn a breath. Her loneliness, her natural enemies among the woodpeckers and bluejays, mark her as the outsider the world punishes, and the mother's reproach of "ingratitude" for resisting birth is the pressure to accept a motherhood and a womanhood unquestioningly, laid on Esther from the first.

The household built "to her mother's size," where everything is "breakable," is the domestic smallness a woman is fitted into, and Esther's harsh childhood, the "deformed foot," the "crossed eyes," the bee that stings her while her mother disbelieves the pain, is the body as the place the self comes apart and the minimizing of female suffering both. Her father's lineage runs prolific and "natural," his mother giving birth "many times, often without knowing it," an instinctive fecundity Esther cannot access, and her mother stands as the "needle's eye" through which the "camel shall not pass," the narrow, excluding femininity Esther is measured against and found wrong.

Rosemary, the stillborn twin, is idealized as "perfect," "considerate," "grateful," the compliant daughter the world would have wanted, and Esther is accused of having "killed a little child before she was ever born." The twin is the illusion of the individual worn by two sisters who are versions of each other, plural selfhood reaching across a womb, and Esther's fixation on Rosemary, her forbidden digging for the grave, is a woman trying to recover the silenced double the family buried, the self she is told she destroyed and cannot stop mourning.

Esther's question of whether she is herself or "the shadow," "the other," is the fracturing of a self the book keeps performing, and her insistence that she is "all flesh, all blood" is an embodied feminism claiming the lived female body against the idealized dead one. Her laughter "shaking the snow from the clouds," her sense that "non-being" is more beautiful than "being," close the chapter on the dissolving boundary between life and death embraced rather than feared, a woman who carries her dead twin and her own contested existence and goes on, defiant and alive, at the threshold the book keeps for its erased.
woman-chapter-01:
Chapter 1

← The Route Down · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 2 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Madge Capehorn · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

The novel puts its thesis on its first pages. On the bus, in the mist, a double-headed man stares into nothing, and the narration turns to the line the whole book will spend eighty-two chapters proving: "every heart is the other heart," "every soul is the other soul." This is the illusion of the individual, stated plainly at the outset, and it is the key to everything that follows. It is larger than a challenge to a male-centered idea of the self. It is the book announcing that separate selfhood is the one illusion it means to dissolve.

The world is going out of focus: "the ghost of the world," "the face of the ambiguous waters," the fading light and mist. This is not a figure for women's uncertain social place. It is the first appearance of real and dream as one country, the book's refusal of any firm line between the seen and the dreamed. The double-headed man is the first body that is already more than one, plural selfhood made literal before the reader has met anyone.

Against this dissolving world stand two poles. Vera's search for Miss MacIntosh, already underway and already without end, is the unfinished quest that will structure the book, and its grief has no bottom. Miss MacIntosh herself is introduced as the one who holds still, a "simple woman with a broken nose" who keeps "truth to nature" and refuses illusion. She is a model of a grounded woman, but the reason the book plants her here, as the least dissolving character it has, is so that her own coming-apart later will carry the most weight. Madge, the pregnant girl painted and adorned over an alienated interior, is the first sketch of the self as a mask or a series of masks or even a series of multiple masks, and of a pregnancy that is already dread rather than promise.

Chapter 17

← Chapter 16 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 18 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

The wig comes off here. Miss MacIntosh stands at the window, her corset stays out like porcupine quills, braced as a "weird wrestler," and then she turns and she is bald, "coldly, stonily bald," a "monster moving toward" Vera in the dark. The stripping of femininity and beauty is the plain surface of the scene, and under it is the body as the place the self comes apart, the red hair gone and with it the woman Vera thought she knew, the "bald pretender" who, Vera realizes, may never have been "herself."

With the hair go the categories. Vera looks at the bald head and sees "an old man," the crossing point arriving on the body the same instant the body is unmade, gender falling away with the wig. The head is "the naked rock lashed by waves," the sea already at Miss MacIntosh even here.

Then the fight, and the fight is with a self that will not hold one shape. Vera grapples a figure that is a fallen angel, a gladiator, a shadow boxer, and finally "no one," a sandbag dummy with an icy untouchable surface. This is fear and violence and control, and it is plural selfhood turned into an opponent, the illusion of the individual made physical: Vera is wrestling something that is many and then nothing, and cannot pin it because there is no single body there to pin. In the morning her hair has been pulled out without pain and her braids are whole, the night both true and undreamed, the real and the dream as one country holding it in both hands.

Chapter 75

← Chapter 74 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 76 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Esther Longtree

Grief opens this chapter as a boundless force beyond control, and the dissolving boundary between life and death runs through it. Esther cannot tell whether the thing she carries is motherhood or "a benign tumor," and the ambiguity is the book's refusal to let the female body be simply read, a pregnancy that hovers between creation and disease, life and its absence. The dead child that haunts her, at once beautiful and terrifying, is the boundary held open around a being neither fully born nor fully gone, the stillborn kept present the way the book keeps all its dead.

A fisherman witnesses her ordeal and cannot be sure what he has seen, and his uncertainty is the world's disbelief of a woman's account, the erasure of her lived reality even by the one who watches it happen. The stillborn thrown into the river is the invisibility of female reproductive loss made literal, a child disposed of into moving water and forgotten, the failure of the record to keep what a woman's body produced and lost, and the normalization of these repeated losses is the town's indifference hardening into Esther's own resignation.

The dead child in her visions is bound to her father, the policeman who patrolled the graveyard, and the intimation of incest folds patriarchal authority into the origin of her suffering, the same man who policed other couples implicated in her own violation. Her dreams of motherhood shade into fear, the marble statue, the uncertainty about what is real, and the confusion is real and dream as one country worked through a woman's reproductive life, the visions as true to her as anything the daylight admits.

At night she crawls and bites and nurses her own fist, feeds an invisible child, and the isolation is the emotional labor of a motherhood no one supports, a woman mothering where the world has left her alone. Yet she keeps her hope against every judgment, refuses to be controlled by the men's narratives, and questions the reproductive justice that would blame her, and her contentment in a hostile world is a quiet reclamation of joy. The chapter closes on a looming war and a society indifferent to the crimes already committed against women, the personal loss and the coming public one set side by side, and Esther enduring at the center of both.
woman-chapter-66:
Chapter 66

← Chapter 65 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 67 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Miss MacIntosh walks into the sea at the end of this chapter, and the dissolving boundary between life and death and the body coming apart carry it there. She meets the day in a whaler's hat and sea boots, braced for storm, regretting she was never a whaler or a fisherman, and the masculine gear and the longing for a man's work are the crossing point worn as clothing and the same refusal of a woman's narrow place she has carried since her story began. Her lessons go on "in spite of death itself," the drilling of Vera against a background of drowned things, suspended time held against the sea's dissolution, and her skepticism of Columbus and Cook and Peary strips the male explorers of their authority even as she prepares to make a crossing none of them charted.

The old Arctic explorer courts her, and his wooden leg set beside her bald head is the shared amputation that binds them, two bodies come apart recognizing each other, the body as the place the self comes apart doubled across a man and a woman. He idealizes the cold, barren, imageless country where there are no calendars and no human faces, and his proposal is for a spiritual rather than a physical union, a marriage past the flesh, and she both feels the pull of his loneliness and refuses to "go with him," choosing self-determination over the escape he offers. The "amputated feet walking by themselves" he imagines are the book's resilience, the self moving forward even stripped of its supports.

She walks into the roaring ocean on a cold morning and does not come back, and the disappearance leaves only fragments, the wig, the corset, the knitting, the practical belongings that outlive her exactly as they did when the book first announced her gone. The sea is her coffin "with no lid but the dream," the boundary between life and death held permanently open the way it has been held open for her since Chapter 3, the law unable to say whether she is dead, the record failing to hold her. The black umbrella moving over water and sand is her enduring, protective presence past her body, and the "wounded doe" standing with a blind eye toward the sea closes the chapter on vulnerability and vigilance together, a woman erased and still, somehow, keeping watch.
woman-chapter-69:
Chapter 69

← Chapter 68 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 70 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Justice O’Leary

The "Fire Escape" room holds the start of this chapter, and invisibility and erasure and the body coming apart run through it. A slop jar of blonde hair combings and a lipstick-stained tobacco flake, a silver church steeple labeled "Forget me not," are the traces of women's presence discarded and half-seen, the erased kept at the threshold the way the book always keeps them. The tattooed landlord fills the space with his own loud story, his happy marriage to a former circus fat lady, his battleship tattoo and his boasts, and his loquaciousness eclipsing the silent women near him is male narrative crowding out female presence, the wife a background figure to the tale a man tells about himself.

His stories run to the grotesque, a mad butcher selling human beings as meat, women preserved as stew, and the commodified and consumed female body is the book's violence carried in a landlord's yarn. The artificial eye he finds in the hangman's pocket, set beside the black poker chip, is the body as the place the self comes apart and the deception under the surface, a false eye and a hidden token where a whole man is supposed to be. The chained buzzards he calls canaries, and Tillie, "a very young girl," knitting a baby hood, hold women's confinement and the early nurturing role side by side, the caged bird and the child already learning to mother.

Dr. Justice O'Leary argues with Sarah, a woman who crawls on the floor and haunts him and will not answer, and his insistence that she is "dead at the age of one," a "dirty baby" with "no tooth in her head," is the interrupted birth returned in the doctor who tended imaginary births, a dead child still present and still refused. Sarah's silence, her refusal to speak or be recognized, is invisibility and erasure worked into a haunting, the woman present and denied, and the boundary between life and death stands open around her exactly as it stands open around Catherine and the coachman, a person the man cannot make either alive or gone.

O'Leary's litany of diseases, his sneer at "Lady Gonorrhea," his fixation on Sarah's beauty and lineage and the "stink of the dead" on her, are the stigmatizing of the female body the book keeps exposing, a woman reduced to shame and contagion and denied the standing to answer. His plan to have "house management" evict her is the institutional machinery for making a woman disappear, and the chapter leaves Sarah crawling and silent and unremoved, the dead child who will not stay dead, kept at the threshold where the book keeps everyone it cannot let the world erase.
woman-chapter-10:
Chapter 10

← Chapter 9 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 11 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Vera cannot picture her own wedding, so she dreams of others', and the one that arrives is impossible on purpose. Mr. Spitzer stands as the bride. Miss MacIntosh, black umbrella in hand, stands as the bridegroom. This is the crossing point in its clearest scene, the place where man and woman trade. The swap is not a trick played on gender norms. It is the book showing that the categories the ceremony depends on, one fixed man and one fixed woman, were never solid to begin with.

The preacher runs the wedding rite and the funeral rite together until neither survives, and the two fuse exactly where this edition's marriage entry says they must. Marriage demands a single, stable self from people who are many, and when the demand meets the book's people it collapses into its opposite, the wedding into the funeral, the boundary between life and death giving way. When the sermon turns to "Oh, woman, where are thy breasts? Where is thy womb?" the gendered body itself is being mourned and unmade, the body coming apart, a line that reaches straight to Miss MacIntosh's own missing breast.

Mr. Spitzer carries the chapter's plural selfhood. He lies in two beds at once, he would "marry no one but his brother worm," and he nods no while he answers yes, a self at odds with itself before the reader has learned how many of him there are. Vera's laughter at the scene is not derision. It is recognition. And her closing fear of the "necromancers" and "old rapists" by the sea, set against her reach for what is "good, true, beautiful" beyond the clouds, is the book's real-and-dream country closing the chapter on the note it keeps: the ordinary world and the dreamed one are one place, and the seam between them is where these people live.
