Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer

Catherine and Mr. Spitzer are set against each other as two ways of knowing, and the gap between them is the chapter's pillar. She lives inside "opium dreams" and "phantasmagoric facts," inventing his life for him out of fragments; he lives by the watch, timing "the music of the dying wind" and the vibrations of bridges, forecasting the natural world into obedience. Her intuitive, dreamlike mode and his measured rational one divide along the old line that assigns reason to men and irrationality to women, and Young turns the assignment over. Catherine's "lack of faith" that "made all things possible to her" is both her powerlessness, the drugged inertia of a woman society has sedated and shelved, and a genuine epistemology, a way of holding the world that his forecasts cannot reach.

Time is the second pillar and it is broken along the same seam. Mr. Spitzer's watches, the ones that keep time and the ones that do not, stand for a male order of measurement, and Catherine's "great coffin of stars" that holds love, her fluid and fragmented sense of duration, refuses to be counted. The shattering of the watch is the shattering of linear time, and it falls on her the way disrupted life-courses fall on women: pregnancy, aging, waiting, the biological and social clocks that mark a woman's body while a man's time runs unburdened. Her opium suspends her between life and death, a "watchful, wide-eyed wakefulness," and this is the boundary held open, neither surrender nor escape but a sovereign province where she rules by seeing what was not there.

Mr. Spitzer's dread of the "fat man" he fears becoming, his anxiety about ridicule and bodily exposure, extends the surveillance of appearance that usually pins women; here it catches him too, and the chapter lets the vulnerability spread across the line rather than stay on one side of it. The closing dissonance, traffic lights "all wrong," the "red light turned to green" at the wrong moment, his near accidents, is the disordered world both of them must cross, and it reads as the mistimed and thwarted chances that meet a woman inside patriarchal time and space. Catherine stays central even while the chapter follows him: her inert body preserves a female consciousness that his rationality can neither wake nor comprehend, and that incomprehension is the point.
woman-a-closing-word:
A closing word

← Decolonization in Miss MacIntosh, My Darling · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus

Characters: Joachim Spitzer

A book about dissolution should be careful how it ends, since an ending is one more boundary, one more line drawn where the argument has spent all its pages rubbing lines out. So this is not a conclusion in the usual sense. It gathers nothing into a fist. It sets the tools down where a reader can pick them up.

Read Miss MacIntosh, My Darling as a book that goes down. Not across, through its famous length, and not around, through its catalog of women's lives, but down, into a mind, until the categories a reader carries in stop holding. Living and dead, waking and dreaming, man and woman, one self and the crowd inside it: the novel does not argue these apart. It stays inside a consciousness long enough that they come apart on their own, the way a word repeated too many times stops meaning anything and becomes only sound. Young found she could reach that depth through any door a woman was handed, the pregnancy, the marriage, the wig, the grief, and that every door opened on the same room. The women are the route. The floor at the bottom of the route has no sex, which is why Mr. Spitzer can stand on it too.

The eleven pillars were never meant to be believed. They are reading tools, and a tool that will not let itself be set down has stopped being a tool and become a doctrine. A reader can grant the premise of this edition, that Young wrote from the seam where the fixed categories give way, and still argue with every single reading in the chapters above. That is the right use of the book. The premise is the ground. The readings are one person's path across it, and other paths are there to be walked.

What stays, when the argument is set aside, is the novel itself, and the novel does not need this edition or any other to be what it is. It was written across eighteen years by a woman who said she thought of herself as neither woman nor man, only as someone doomed to write, and who was met for saying so with the particular rage a culture keeps for those who will not stay sorted. She wrote from that rage's target and did not flinch from it. She put down what happens to a woman, all of it, and then went underneath what happens to a woman to the structure of a self under pressure, and there she wrote what the whole book keeps saying to anyone who will hear it. “Every heart is the other heart. Every soul is the other soul. The individual is the one illusion.”

That is not a comfort and it was not offered as one. It is a finding, arrived at through fiction before there was a settled language to name it, and it belongs now to whoever reads far enough to reach it. The women Young kept at the threshold, the erased and the unfinished and the unheard, are still there in the book, still enduring, still refusing to disappear. This edition has tried only to say, in the plainest terms it could find, where to stand to see them, and then to get out of the way.

The links that follow lead further into the reading. They are there for the reader who wants to keep going down.

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

By morning the wig is back on. Miss MacIntosh greets the day as a sailor, "heave ho, my hearties!", landlocked and over-dressed and entirely sure of the performance, the "red marcelled top" restored over the bald head, the false teeth in, the usual being reassembled piece by piece. This is her no-nonsense cheer, and it is the self as mask put back on in daylight, the assembled person the book has just shown Vera how to take apart.

She reads the newspapers aloud, drills Vera on biblical genealogies, sets the rare china on the table, and declares she "would not give a grain of salt" for ghosts, that she keeps to "essential facts." This is her grounded realism, and it is her standing as the anti-dream, the pole that refuses the country Catherine lives in, made poignant now because the reader has watched the dream reach her own door. Her fury at the calendar reform that disrupted "our schedule" and moved the day of worship is her love of order, and it is the book's suspended time seen from the side that wants the hours to hold still.

Underneath the performance runs a small erasure. She never asks Vera about the bruises and scratches of the night, never inquires after her at all, and Vera's interior goes unseen across the breakfast table, the girl present and unregarded while the older woman performs the day.

Characters: Gertrude Hathaway Tidings · Joachim Spitzer · Madge Capehorn · Moses Hunnecker · Musidora Tidings

The chapter opens on Moses and "old Doc" again, and the doctor as a failed male authority. He is also better understood as the continuation of Chapter 5's central image. He answers calls that never come, drives a car that cannot move, and presides over a country where, as the text says, there are no births and no deaths. This is the interrupted birth widened into a whole landscape, and the boundary between life and death held permanently open: a place where nothing completes, neither the arrival nor the departure.

Gertrude, who married two brothers and is said to have "killed two brothers with one stone," is the first appearance of a figure the book will make central in Mr. Spitzer, the two brothers who are versions of one another, so alike that a single act reaches both. The doubling is plural selfhood, worn by minor characters before the major one arrives.

Musidora, Gertrude's sister, mute and childlike and sold by her mother for sixteen dollars as the neglected poor woman. She is that and she is also the book's recurring figure at the edge of erasure, the person present and almost unseen, almost unheard, who returns as the literal mute of the later chapters. When Madge says Musidora "will be always with us," the line is not only social pity. It is the book naming what it does with the erased: it keeps them, present and unaccounted for, at the threshold. The children eating in the graveyard hold that threshold too, life carrying on among the graves.
woman-youngs-contribution-to-feminist-th:
Young's contribution to feminist thought

← Woman's Experiences · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Decolonization in Miss MacIntosh, My Darling →

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Esther Longtree · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh

Marguerite Young's contribution to feminism is easy to undersell, because on its face the novel looks like a catalog: the practical nursemaid, the opium-dreaming mother, the perpetually pregnant waitress, the militant suffrage captain, a spectrum of female lives laid end to end. Read that way the book adds range to feminist literature and little else. The contribution is deeper and stranger than range. Young takes the female condition down to the level of consciousness, to the place where the self comes apart, and what she finds there has no gender. Women are her route in and not her subject at the bottom. She could reach that floor through women because their selfhood had already been broken open by their conditions, and the breaking apart the culture had done to them was the opening she needed. This is how a novel so uninterested in programming still enlarges the feminist tradition: it reads what happens to women all the way down, past the social surface to the structure of a self under pressure, and that structure belongs to everyone.

The vocabulary this edition uses for that structure, the pillars of a Radical Immanence, is contemporary, offered as a description of what the novel enacts and not as a philosophy Young held. The claim is that she arrived at these forms through fiction before the language existed to name them, and that her women are where the forms are clearest because the women were already living them.

Miss MacIntosh looks like the book's plainest feminist figure, and she is: the disdain for jewels and furs and superficial beauty is a real critique of a womanhood built on appearance, and her groundedness, her labor, her care for the poor and the working and the marginalized, ties that critique to a wider demand for justice. But her deepest work is not the critique. It is the wig lifted off the bald head, the amputated breast, the self stripped to its substance, the "porcelain crown" she says is under every face. She is the character built to look most single, and she comes apart most completely, and the stripping is revelation rather than punishment, a woman taken down to the body as the place the self comes apart and shown to be, at that depth, simply a human creature under the covering everyone wears.

Catherine reads as idealized feminine passivity decaying into loss of agency, a caution against beauty and dependence. She is more than a caution. She is scattered across her dream-guests, found in a mountain range and a pharaoh and a stranger's reflection and no single self called Catherine, and her opium twilight is the fullest case in the book of a person held on both sides of the line between living and dead at once. Her dissolution is plural selfhood and real and dream as one country, and it is not the failure of a woman so much as a consciousness gone deep enough that the categories holding a self together give way.

Esther Longtree carries the female body's burdens as the repeated pregnancies, the stillbirths, the social judgment, and she carries something under them. Her perpetual pregnancy that never delivers is the interrupted birth, which is unfinished-is-not-failed and permanent grief in the same body, the self that cannot complete and the sorrow that has no bottom. The reproductive politics are real and they are not the floor. The floor is a condition the old doctor's phantom deliveries and the wild mares bearing "waters and winds" carried before Esther ever did, a shape of consciousness that takes a woman's flesh here because a woman's flesh is where it shows.

Cousin Hannah is the radical feminist icon, the suffrage captain who fought "the overthrow of man," and she is also the woman "disguised as an Arab king," the "secret man" within women made a whole figure, the person the record keeps failing to hold. Her militancy and her dissolution of the fixed self are one motion. She is the crossing point given a biography, and her feminism is inseparable from the fact that she will not stay one sex, one identity, one thing the record can file.

Mr. Spitzer is the proof the frame reaches past gender, and putting him beside the women is the argument. He cannot tell which brother he is, he thins out toward transparency, he reaches the same coming-apart the women reach, by a different door. If the floor Young reaches through women were female at the bottom, he could not stand on it, and he does. What breaks a woman open in this book is what breaks anyone open. The women are the route because history had already done the breaking apart to them, not because the thing at the end of the route is theirs alone.

This is why the illusion of the individual is not a spiritual dimension added onto feminism but the bottom the feminism reaches. The interconnectedness the novel keeps stating, "every heart is the other heart," is what Young finds when she goes through the female self far enough, and it is the same whether a woman or a man arrives at it. The dissolution of the self is not a separate philosophical layer laid over the portraits of women. It is what the portraits are for.

Young said she never thought of herself as either a woman or a man, only as a person born to be a writer. That could be understood as a writer keeping her distance from feminism. Here, it is the thesis in the author's own mouth: she wrote from the crossing point. And the "rage against women" she met from reviewers, the men who "seemed to want to destroy" her and her writing, is what happens to a writer who refuses the category the culture insists on, evidence of the cost and not a contradiction of the claim.

Young's feminism, then, is a feminism of consciousness. She does not argue for women so much as go through them, down to the place where the self a woman is made to perform comes apart, and there she finds the structure that holds for anyone. That is her original contribution, and it is why the book belongs to feminism and exceeds it in the same breath. It honors the specific weight the world lays on women, and it follows that weight all the way to the floor where it stops being only theirs.

Chapter 6

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Homer Capehorn · Jacqueline White · Madge Capehorn · Miss MacIntosh

Madge's long chapter is where the book first shows a self coming apart in real time. It is the coming-apart as a catalog of what patriarchy does to women and the structure underneath it is plural selfhood. Madge is "herself and the other," she is "breaking into two," her thoughts run "like a mouse in an intricate cage," and when she dances she dances "with her shadow." She is not one person suffering through an institution. She is a person the book has already split, and the splitting is the subject.

Marriage is where the split is forced, and the chapter treats it as the demand that a divided self perform as one. Madge's marriage is "empty and hollow and ghostly," the wedding bells are funeral bells, the "circle of creation" is a wedding ring and a grave at once. It is marriage as social death and it runs the wedding and the funeral together, the same fusion Chapter 10 will stage openly, so that marriage becomes the place where the boundary between living and dead gives way. The "dead child dancing" and the grinning skull under Madge's painted face are that boundary made visible.

Her resistance to the pregnancy belongs to the interrupted birth. She would give birth, she says, only "to an urn, to a stone angel," and she is "coming to her early grave"; the pregnancy is dread and the birth is death, the shape the book gives every pregnancy it touches. The armor she fashions against all this, the "golden mail" and "mailed gloves," is the self as mask, the same armor Miss MacIntosh wears as helmet-hair and corset.

The chapter's long meditation on Jacqueline White, the dying rival, is where the illusion of the individual surfaces. The men's love for Jacqueline is "lost in a crowd," the triangle of Madge, Homer, and the dead girl keeps folding into new triangles, and Homer reframes death itself as "birth" and eternal youth. It is the male denial of female mortality and love with no single object, selves that will not stay distinct, and death and birth trading places. Homer is not failing to understand Madge. He is speaking the book's thesis without knowing it.

Chapter 8

← Chapter 7 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 9 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Beatrice Fitzgerald · Moses Hunnecker

Two roads run through this chapter, and the difference between them is the book's difference. On one, the graveyard, the family names worn off the stones, the "dead ear," and "no sound but the past." On the other, a "beautiful life" where children dance and youth and age are suspended. It is a feminist utopia outside time's cruelty and suspended time, the book's dream-country where the clock does not run, set against the effaced names of erasure on the road that death still governs.

Beatrice Fitzgerald, gossiped over for her reputation and her illegitimate son, is going blind, "losing the other eye." She is a marginalized woman rendered invisible and also the deaf-and-blind motif again, erasure through a severed sense, the same thread as the deaf villagers of Chapter 4 and the blindness that runs through the book. Moses's tirade against "old Doc" and against aging, the "change of life" and "mortal corruption," carries the body coming apart in a lower, comic register.

The spectral village that closes the chapter, its "dead souls," its "men whose heads do grow beneath their shoulders," its "dream within the dream," is real and dream as one country at its densest so far. The rearranged bodies are plural selfhood in a grotesque key. It is an image of women's social erasure and the dissolving ordinary shape of a person and a place, and it is doing it to everyone in view.
woman-chapter-50:
Chapter 50

← Chapter 49 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 51 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Joachim Spitzer

The universe will not hold still in this chapter, and its instability is the pillar. A "snow bird" veers in the wind, "central fires of jewels" flicker, "relationships which were never to be found" dissolve among a multiplicity of "mirrors" and "phases," and the woman's uncertain place in the world and the plural, unfixed self arrive as one shifting weather. Mr. Spitzer loses himself in "clouded rooms," "one room so like the other," a "rose withering in a vase where there had been no rose before," two golden chairs of which one may be only a dream, and the doubling that will not resolve is the illusion of the individual seen from inside a mind coming apart.

Instruments without strings run through the chapter, "a lyre without strings, a trumpet without a throat," and Mr. Spitzer fears he is himself "only the dream," an "imaginary bird" caught in the strings. This silencing and loss of expressive power is invisibility and erasure and it is the music that goes unheard, the instrument unstrung, the voice with no throat. His complaint against God for making "dice without markings," for a life lived "by the dreams of others," is women's imposed passivity and it is the book's larger claim that no self authors itself, each living inside another's dream.

The "beautiful opium lady" holds the chapter's center, chattering "madly," her "imaginary dawns" and her inability to "keep a chart of time's dimensions" or to tell life from death making her the fullest figure of a woman held between the two, real and dream as one country ruled from a drugged bed. Mr. Spitzer's return to her, "body and soul and spirit crying in the wind," and his faith that "when life was over, it would begin" on a star where "living love was united with dead love," is dependency and longing and it is the dissolving boundary reached toward as a home, the place where the categories of living and dead finally give way. Her "disassociations and mistakes of senses" are her powerlessness and her way of knowing at once, the two never separated.

The star toward which the chapter reaches is a "keyhole star," a "door of truth" "never opened by man," where "no eye stared on either side," and the woman's exclusion from knowledge and the self's exclusion from its own truth are one locked door. Life is "scarcely understood before it was gone," a "flying sand grain" becoming a star, and "all that happened happened only once," the irretrievability that falls hardest on women. The chapter ends on the "old suffragette captain" from whom Mr. Spitzer "had learned much," her "hyphenated name more important than the two names it joined," her "broken melody" she would not "take up in life but perhaps in death," a woman whose fulfillment was deferred past living, her mind dying before her heart, and the "nocturne" written for her is the unheard song the book keeps composing for its erased.
woman-chapter-31:
Chapter 31

← Chapter 30 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 32 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer

Cousin Hannah is a woman the record cannot hold, and that failure of the record is the chapter's pillar. Mr. Spitzer's every attempt to reach her, the unanswered doors, the letters, the uncertainty about her name and dates and even her existence, is the erasure of women's histories enacted in real time, the patriarchal archive unable to contain a woman who lived outside its categories. She rides "through deserts and mountains alone, shrouded in purple and gold," beyond the reach of male bureaucracy, and her elusiveness is not an accident but the shape of her autonomy.

Her feminism is stated plainly and lived hard. She is the suffragist who marched "through snow, deserts, and forbidden cities," who confronts "Persian lions, sheiks, African kings, Turks," whose battles are literal and figurative at once. She never married, carried "a great secret," and lived a nomadic life outside marriage and domesticity; her refusal to commemorate Peron's suicide, her indifference to Catherine's lawyer, are refusals of the emotional economies that bind women to men through mourning and memory. This is radical female agency and it is the difficulty of narrating a life the culture has no form for, the same difficulty.

Mr. Spitzer's imagined epitaphs gather the paradox. He honors a warrior "who fought many battles" yet "could not save herself" from "the domestic war" and "mortal frailty," and the balance of public valor and private vulnerability is the whole trouble of a feminist life told in words made by others. His hesitation to finish the epitaph, his legalistic effort to pin her identity, is patriarchal management failing to capture the fullness of a woman who lived past its documentation. Hannah's scorn for "the external man" and "the phantoms of the air," her "oath" against men and rivals, closes the chapter on a woman who has broken with dependency altogether, and the record keeps failing to hold her, which is exactly her victory.
woman-chapter-47:
Chapter 47

← Chapter 46 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 48 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer

The two shores organize this chapter, and the crossing between them is the pillar. Cousin Hannah, the "great suffrage captain," lies dead with the mountains for a tomb, her blood on the snow, and the narration wonders about a child "red as her blood, white as the snow" and then about itself: "Could I have been a woman, could I have been a man." The suffrage struggle raised to myth and the crossing point arrive together, gender coming loose at the graveside of the woman who fought hardest against its fixities. Mr. Spitzer defers his own life to the next, imagining a "night of love" that makes "no distinction between living and dead, lover and loved," the dissolving boundary and the illusion of the individual folded into one wish.

The doubling runs the chapter. Mr. Spitzer and his dead brother Peron are twins, and Peron's laughter keeps breaking into "his music of total harmony or his silence," the brother's disorder intruding on the brother's order the way it always does. The brother stands on the far shore as a "Welcoming Committee," greeting the captain into a "colony under no flag," and the flagless colony is the book's utopia past every sorting nation and category, the place where the crossings the living forbid are simply the weather. Plural selfhood is the ground of it: Spitzer cannot say which brother he is, whether he is dead or alive, and the not-knowing is not his failure but the book's truth surfacing in its central man.

His frailty against Peron's idealization of "deathless beauty and purity" is the tension the book keeps between aging flesh and the fantasy that would freeze women young, and Spitzer's blurred vision, his difficulty telling near from far, is the fractured self trying to locate itself among conflicting demands. He grows "transparent," "worn," shedding papers, composing fragmentary music, and the transparency is invisibility and erasure worked on the witness himself, the man who preserves lost histories thinning until he is one of the lost. The music "none had heard," the "dead Troubadour," the "lady never awakening," are the unheard song the book keeps playing for whoever is deaf to it.

Snowflakes whisper human voices and name themselves "kings, queens, clowns, and shahs," the multiplicity and fluidity of the self scattered into weather, and Mr. Spitzer doubts the captain "had ever found her love," calls her "ambiguous and never easily defined," which is unfulfilled feminist longing and the refusal of a fixed self held in one phrase. Death arrives as a "dipping sail," "a moment of rapture forever prolonged," and the captain dies "with none to uphold her," solitary at the end of a public life. The planetary wheel turns over "roads no traveller had ever travelled," there is no "master key" and always a missing "factor," and the chapter closes on marriage as "no by-road" but a passage straight to death, the "opium lady" and the "old corsair" "hacked by many wounds" gathered at the edge of it, every woman's survival scarred and every crossing still open.
woman-chapter-72:
Chapter 72

← Chapter 71 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 73 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Esther Longtree · Miss MacIntosh

Esther Longtree arrives in this chapter, and the interrupted birth she carries is the book's oldest shape given at last its fullest body. She is "everlastingly pregnant," swelling toward deliveries that end in stillbirth and miscarriage and, at the extreme, "the birth of nothing," and the pregnancy that will not complete, which the old doctor and the wild mares and the empty country all carried before her, is here made flesh in a waitress at the "Greasy Spoon." The hearse and the old grey mule halted outside, the mural of birds with human faces, set the boundary between life and death open before she speaks, a diner where the funeral procession stops and the dead and the living take their coffee together.

Her body is the book's plainest catalog of coming-apart, the swelling that never resolves, the bald spot spreading on her head, the loose hair, the heart "leaking like the sky," and Esther's flesh rejects the ideal the way Miss MacIntosh's bald head rejects it, the body as the place the self comes apart worn openly and even with humor. She is lonely, without romantic love, the sterile "fathers" absent or indifferent, and she knits garments "without needles or thread" for children who will not arrive, the maternal creativity and the maternal loss carried in the same empty hands.

Her memory reaches back to wild mares "pregnant without males," bearing "waters and winds," and the mares are the interrupted birth widened into a female fecundity that owes nothing to men, generation independent of the fathers who fail her, a mystical creation set against the sterile salesmen and the disbelieving town. Esther's sustained pregnancy despite every disbelief is the book insisting on a woman's experience the world refuses to see, invisibility and erasure met by a body that will not stop being pregnant no matter who denies it.

At the chapter's end Esther nurses her own clenched fist beside the lost children and asks "Who killed cock robin?", answering that "all people killed him," and the answer is the diffusion of agency the book stated at the start, a death with no single author, the same logic that would not say who killed Miss MacIntosh now spread across every loss Esther bears. Her "Never, never" is her refusal of the guilt the world would pin on her alone, a woman declining to be the single hand behind a violence the whole world commits, and the chapter leaves her pregnant and luminous and unaccounted for, the fullest figure the book has yet made of the birth that will not come.
woman-chapter-29:
Chapter 29

← Chapter 28 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 30 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Joachim Spitzer

Boundaries will not hold in this chapter, and their refusal is the pillar. Mr. Spitzer cannot fix the line between butterfly and moth, day-flier and night-flier, and the exceptions to every rule keep multiplying until classification itself looks like a wish rather than a fact. The blurred categories carry the weight of gender: the same skepticism that dissolves butterfly and moth dissolves the fixed binary of man and woman, and Young's natural history becomes an argument against essentialism, the fixed positions patriarchy calls natural shown to be exceptions all the way down.

Metamorphosis is the pillar's second face. The caterpillar's passage through the chrysalis, "likened to sleep or death," is transformation and rebirth, the protected interval a self needs to grow, and it reads as the confinement a woman passes through before she emerges freer. The sexual dimorphism Mr. Spitzer notes, the perfumed male and the scentless female, restages the old arrangement in which men are active and women passive or unseen, the male wing scented to draw a female who waits; his sense that the perfume is "the perfume of his thoughts" turns the arrangement into something internalized, a gendered order living inside perception.

Against that order Young sets the feminine divine. The butterflies named for goddesses, for "the goddess of the moon, goddess of wisdom," recover a female power the dominant religious frame has buried, and the cosmic butterflies that predate earthly life make female creativity foundational rather than secondary. Mr. Spitzer's solitary, introspective attention to these creatures is the inner life patriarchal culture overlooks, and his oscillation between light and darkness, life and death, is the liminal ground the chapter prefers to any settled category. The refusal of fixed categories and the reclamation of feminine power are one motion, and the chapter ends inside that motion, in a world of multiplicity and change rather than fixed and hierarchical kinds.
woman-chapter-33:
Chapter 33

← Chapter 32 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 34 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer

A Boston newspaper calls Catherine "the late Mrs. Catherine Cartwheel," "a famous beauty of the past," while she is still alive, and that error is the chapter's pillar: the boundary between life and death held open, a woman reported dead because she no longer performs youth and visibility. The mistake is society's habit of consigning women to the past once they stop conforming, and Catherine's persistence past her own obituary is a quiet insistence that she is not finished being.

Mr. Spitzer's choice not to correct the paper leaves her narrative in male hands, the "opium taker in love with her starry illusions" managed by a benevolent man who will not disturb her, and this is patriarchal control of a woman's story. Yet the chapter turns the drugged, dreamlike mode into a genuine freedom. Catherine's memories of her wedding, fragmented and defiant of chronology, her marriages "to Death" or to abstractions rather than to a man, refuse the bridal narrative and the patriarchal claim that a woman's legitimacy hinges on marriage. Her rejection of Mr. Spitzer as a suitor even while he stands present is a critical stance against male-defined relationship, and her "beautifully inaccurate" memory becomes a mode of knowing that his precision, his watch and his measured wind, cannot reach.

That contrast of her irrational "greater freedom" against his obsession with control is the gendered epistemology the novel keeps returning to, reason assigned to men and dream to women, and Young revaluing the dream. Catherine's unconsciousness offers "improbable possibility" where his rationality offers only foreclosure. The chapter closes with her conversing with a blackbird, detached from patriarchal reality and logic, and Mr. Spitzer opening the door to let the bird in, a tentative male accommodation of a female subjectivity he cannot rationalize. The boundary stays open, and her refusal to conform to the world's report of her death is the freedom the chapter finally credits.

Chapter 21

← Chapter 20 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 22 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

The bald head becomes an image the chapter turns over slowly, a "moon sunken beyond a watery horizon," "the secret pearl," the thing under "the palpable disguise of the average man." This is the loss of the feminine beauty tied to hair, and it is the body as the place the self comes apart raised to a general law: the baldness is not Miss MacIntosh's private wound but the truth under the disguise every person wears, the face left when the covering is gone. Vera means to hide it so Miss MacIntosh can stay "a usual being in the light," the tender concealment from the last chapter carried forward, the mask kept on for love.

Miss MacIntosh, "incapable of grand or feeble impersonations or plain hypocrisies," is nonetheless the one who says that "evil has many forms, and the good has only one and has no other face." The line is her plain morality, and it is the book's arithmetic of the self, the many faces the novel keeps finding set against the single face it almost never does. Her warning to "not be easily deceived by fine feathers which make fine birds" is the same thought worn as country wisdom.

Vera's pity settles on the body itself, "the stalk of a breast which had been cut away so early," "the scar," "no eyebrows, no eyelashes," and the chapter honors the "denudement of the substance" rather than flinching from it. When the ruined party dress is thrown out for good, "There'll be no new one," the ornamental self goes with it, the filmy floating disguise discarded so the plain, unmasked person can stand where it stood.
woman-chapter-48:
Chapter 48

← Chapter 47 · Woman in Young's Magnum Opus · Chapter 49 →

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Peron Spitzer

Keys open this chapter and open nothing, and the failed key is its pillar. Mr. Spitzer, caught between worlds with a duty half legal and half musical, fumbles at locks; a woman returns from "suffrage journeys and wars" with "forty keys" to open her trunks and find a "nesting place"; and the keys that will not turn are women's dispossession under the law and the book's larger locksmithing, the "arrowsmith" one would need "to reach the dead heart," the "no master key" that recurs whenever a self proves unopenable. Widows appear early, wronged by "cruel husbands and lords," and their liberation from patriarchal imprisonment is figured as trunks that need forty keys, freedom stored behind locks a woman must carry herself.

Love fades and is not noticed fading, the "dead love not awakening" replaced by "a stranger," and the widow's emotional labor going unseen is invisibility and erasure in the register the book reserves for women's inner lives. Loyalty still holds "through all the hazards of disappointment," a resilience the chapter credits, and Mr. Spitzer's contrast with Peron's reckless, fiery life, the "matches" and "burning," sets a thoughtful, vulnerable manhood against the bravado the book keeps deflating. Consciousness, death, and love cross their boundaries here as everywhere, real and dream as one country, and the house fills with "mirror images which had dissolved," selves that reflected once and no longer hold.

The chapter thins Mr. Spitzer toward nothing. His clothing is a "backless suit," his "cape full of holes," and his fear of being seen "as he was" is the body as the place the self comes apart, the vulnerability under the costume the same one the wig and the corset hid on Miss MacIntosh. He passes "through a keyhole" and is "translated," and the passage is the crossing point turned metaphysical: born "after the moon set and dying before the moon arose," he questions whether he and his brother are "one and the same," male and female selves merging as the constellations lose their "glittering feathers" and the "great abyss" swallows "moons, suns, stars." The lamplighter and the ferryman, the "old bookkeeper" balancing accounts in a dream on a "bridge between two worlds," are the roles a self takes when it will not stay single.

The chapter ends inside ice and inversion. "Incorruptible dreams" freeze into "human landscapes," and the "beautiful ladies" are frozen into "ancient patriarchs," "the fathers of this world," ladies with "bearded faces" and "patriarchal robes." This is the crossing point at its most literal, women and men trading faces in the ice, and it is the subversion of patriarchal authority the book keeps performing, the fathers revealed to be beautiful ladies underneath, the categories fluid all the way down. The frozen scene preserves the inversion the way ice preserves anything, holding gender's collapse where the reader can look at it.
